kept.heading: EXPERIENTIAL MARKETING TREND: BRAND GAZETTES (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Brand gazettes are becoming a way for brands to extend physical events into tangible content experiences. Publications are designed specifically for an activation and give attendees something to read and keep after the event. Grey Goose used its Gazette to tell stories about the brand's French heritage while Disney recreated the fictional Runway magazine from The Devil Wears Prada 2 as a real 90-page issue. QR codes and other interactive elements can also connect print content to digital experiences.
kept.article_text:
Title: Experiential Marketing Trend of the Week: Brand Gazettes

URL Source: https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/experiential-marketing-trend-of-the-week-brand-gazettes/

Published Time: 2026-10-05T12:00:03+00:00

Markdown Content:
[Trend of the Week](https://www.eventmarketer.com/category/trend-of-the-week/ "Trend of the Week archive")

Monday, October 5, 2026

![Image 1](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/bobbi-brown-newsstand-2026-eventmarketer-3.jpg)

 Photo: Courtesy of Bobbi Brown 

The digital age has turned physical newspapers into something of a novelty, and event profs are taking advantage by printing their own publications, and treating them as fresh engagement tools.

Whether it’s Grand Central Terminal or the shores of Cannes, the curated periodicals are popping up at a host of events, operating as a form of educational swag and a tangible keepsake. From custom recipes to thought leadership to partner spotlights to [product insights](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/brief-voice-of-logan-pampered-with-love/) and beyond, here’s what’s circulating in brand gazettes.

### **The Goose Gazette**

Various issues of Grey Goose’s _The Goose Gazette_ have been printed this year, including during the US Open at the brand’s “[Last Serve Bar](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/rolling-coverage-brand-experiential-2026-us-open/)” activation, and as part of its Grey Goose Hôtel experience in Picardie, France.

For the hotel takeover, [the publication](https://www.instagram.com/p/DWkG5seACSc/?img_index=1) was themed around the brand’s roots in Picardie, where it harvests the wheat for its vodka. The issue included info on Grey Goose’s French heritage, its global launches, recommendations for cocktails to drink in key European summer locations, and QR codes that linked to everything from a curated playlist to a Paris travel guide.

### **Hot Wheels Zine**

For its inaugural Class of Legends campaign, Hot Wheels recruited music star Maluma, content creator Supercar Blondie and soccer champ Robert Lewandowski to each serve as a “legend” and co-design a limited-edition die-cast car.

To give the program a boost, the Mattel-owned brand hosted a pop-up in Venice, CA, at the end of August. In addition to life-size Hot Wheels cars and giveaways, the event included the debut of [_Hot Wheels Zine_](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdHN2sqDpv8/), the brand’s first-ever print magazine. The content spanned exclusive interviews with the legends, design insights and car culture stories.

### **Yes, And**

SheaMoisture’s _Yes, And_ magazine is all about celebrating the multidimensionality of Black women, and this year for the third edition, the brand incorporated the publication into its[Sheaversity on the Yard](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdBxRtMHEad/?hl=en&img_index=1) HBCU campus experience as a “storytelling companion” to the activation at five schools.

For the special HBCU issues (one for each school), the brand partnered with campus ambassadors, and showcased their personal stories, leadership journeys, community participation, haircare needs, favorite products and how they navigate self-expression.

### **Runway, IRL**

Disney rolled out an experiential [marketing blitz](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/the-devil-wears-prada-2-experiential-marketing-campaign/) to tease “The Devil Wears Prada 2” over the summer that included pop-ups in six cities anchored by a larger-than-life high-heel installation, and supported by interactive touchpoints.

[![Image 2](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/diseny-devil-wears-prada-2-red-heel-tour-2026-eventmarketer-mag.jpg)](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/diseny-devil-wears-prada-2-red-heel-tour-2026-eventmarketer-mag.jpg)

Photo: Courtesy of Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures

Among them: The fictional magazine from the movie franchise, _Runway_, which for the first time ever was designed, printed and released as a real, 90-plus-page issue displayed on a [newsstand](https://www.instagram.com/p/DXFzwDvDydx/) next to the heel.

The publication featured Emily Blunt on the cover as her character Emily Charlton. Inside, were spreads highlighting fashion influencers and content creators, including Young Emperors and Ethan Mundt (aka Utica Queen).

### **The Amazon Ads Gazette**

At Cannes Lions 2026, Amazon’s Port experience encompassed a French village-themed footprint with “storefronts” set up along “Le Boulevard d’Amazon” representing its different properties.

Nestled among them was a newsstand installation displaying copies of _[The Amazon Ads Gazette](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/cannes-lions-2026-experiential/)_ (printed as “La Gazette des Partenaires”), a publication featuring thought leadership and tactical insights from 30 partners.

### **Music, Fashion, Film Tour**

As part of Dove’s sponsorship of Charli xcx’s summertime Music, Fashion, Film Tour, the brand crafted its own tabloid-style [newspaper](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/brief-friskies-cat-lectibles-cheez-it-court/) and showcased it on newsstands in three cities while touting its Whole Body Deo as the solution to sweaty concerts.

At each activation, the first 300 people in line scored a limited-edition Dove x Charli xcx newspaper with exclusive photography of the artist on tour, and featuring Peel & Reveal stickers that rewarded dozens of fans with a pair of free tickets to a tour show.

Talk about breaking news.

* * *

kept.heading: CASH-STRAPPED AMERICANS TAP HOME EQUITY AND AI TO KEEP SPENDING (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Consumers are maintaining spending despite higher prices by finding ways to offset rising costs. Grocery prices are up 32% since 2020, yet spending on cars, clothing, and restaurants still increased in August. Some consumers are using credit or drawing from savings while others are cutting costs elsewhere. AI is also becoming a budgeting tool, with one consumer using ChatGPT to compare grocery prices and save about $100 a month.
kept.article_text:
Title: Cash-Strapped Americans Tap Home Equity and AI to Keep Spending

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/DdAI31

Published Time: 2026-10-03T14:00:03.911Z

Markdown Content:
For the past five months, prices have been rising faster than wages, a turnabout that might have pushed US consumers to cut back. Instead, they’ve kept spending.

Consumption rose at the [fastest pace](https://blinks.bloomberg.com/news/stories/TM6JOZKK3NYA "Bloomberg story") in over a year in August, with government data this week showing increases in categories such as cars, clothing and restaurants.

To keep it going, households across the income spectrum are drawing on a wide range of resources: tapping into the equity they’ve built in their homes, going to food banks to free up money for other purchases or using ChatGPT to lower grocery bills.

It’s something Tom Barkin, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, is seeing in company earnings reports and as he talks to businesses and people around his district, which spans from Maryland to South Carolina.

“As things get a little tighter, as prices go up and challenge wage growth, people do want to maintain their lifestyle,” Barkin said in an interview. “I’ve just been taken by the resourcefulness of the consumer.”

In Atlanta’s northern suburbs, Elizabeth Gentile, 61, and her husband haven’t necessarily had to cut back, but they’ve always lived below their means. Now, with gas prices averaging more than $4 a gallon across the country, the couple is employing a trick at their local Kroger, a technique some have dubbed the “double fill up.”

They’ll park two family cars on either side of Kroger’s gas pumps and hand the dispenser off to their spouse when done, keeping it to a single transaction and eligible for up to a dollar off per gallon.

“If a car pulls up while we are gassing, we always explain to them what we are doing to be courteous,” Gentile said. “We laugh and say that we are sharing our dollar-off fuel points. So far everyone has understood.”

The US is in its sixth year of inflation that central bankers like Barkin — and many Americans — deem too high.

The cost of groceries is up 32% since the start of 2020, with a pound of ground beef now averaging a [record $7.16](https://blinks.bloomberg.com/news/stories/TL5K02KJH6V4 "Bloomberg story"). Households have been hit by a succession of price shocks triggered by the post-pandemic boom, tariffs and now a war in Iran. Wages aren’t keeping up anymore: They have trailed price growth since March, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

An employee prepares ground beef for a customer in Washington.Photographer: Stefani Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images

The situation is frustrating consumers, with sentiment hovering near a record low set earlier this year. Yet a recent analysis of quarterly company earnings by Bloomberg Economics and Bloomberg Intelligence found that consumer health has [improved somewhat](https://blinks.bloomberg.com/news/stories/TLU2QGKGZAL1 "Click to view webpage.") in spite of it all.

Large retailers including Walmart Inc. are reporting that some customers are [trading down](https://blinks.bloomberg.com/news/stories/TK17C3KJH6V7 "Click to view webpage."), seeking discounts and turning to store-brand products that are less expensive than brand-name goods. But Darden Restaurants Inc.’s chief executive also said last month that people keep [coming back](https://blinks.bloomberg.com/news/stories/TLVFGCPR0075 "Click to view webpage.") to his casual-dining chains, which include Olive Garden.

### Resourceful Consumers

To fund that spending, the resourcefulness noted by the Richmond Fed’s Barkin runs the gamut. One way are buy-now-pay-later services, which have exploded in popularity, particularly among young people, and have grown about 20% every year since 2021, according to [research](https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief/2026/eb_26-05 "Research") from the regional Fed.

Kenny Marbry, a teacher from Atlanta’s Duluth suburb, seized on artificial intelligence tools. He’ll feed grocery store receipts into ChatGPT to evaluate whether Kroger or Sam’s Club is the better option or snap pictures of a store’s entire shelf to let AI evaluate the best deals.

Marbry, 38, figures he’s saving around $100 a month with help from his chatbot assistant, as well as some extra discipline he’s picked up comparison-shopping.

“I’m much more likely now to look at a price and ask myself, ‘Do I really need to buy this? Can I get it somewhere else cheaper? Or can I make it myself?’,” Marbry said. “Those small decisions add up, especially when you’re feeding a family of five and trying to make every dollar stretch.”

For others, food banks are becoming a go-to to free up money for other necessities.

“Housing assistance, rental assistance, that’s very difficult to get. Food is a lot easier,” said Brian Greene, head of the Houston Food Bank, the country’s largest by distribution.

The buzz among many automotive body shops is that cash-strapped consumers are living with the dings and dents on their cars and forgoing repairs, said Aaron Schulenburg, executive director of the Society of Collision Repair Specialists. That’s at least partly because of surging insurance costs. Deductibles of $2,000 are no longer unheard of, he said.

“They’re facing financial decisions where in other periods of time, when people were stretched less, it was an easier decision to go get their cars fixed,” Schulenburg said.

Shell-shocked by new car prices that are averaging [$50,000](https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/august-2026-atp-report/ "Cox Automotive data"), Americans are taking on longer-term loans to afford the monthly bill. In August, 31.3% of vehicle loans had terms longer than six years, a record in data from automotive services firm Cox Automotive and up 5.8 percentage points from a year earlier.

A customer looks at a new vehicle at a dealership in Thousand Oaks, California.Photographer: Jill Connelly/Bloomberg

“It’s a reminder that it’s always the monthly payment that people are thinking about,” said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox. “It’s quite astonishing. They’re going, ‘What can you do to get to that monthly payment to make this work?’”

### Investments, Home Equity

More affluent consumers are drawing from assets that have boomed post-pandemic. The share of people making net withdrawals from their investment accounts has doubled since 2019, a JPMorganChase Institute [report](https://www.jpmorganchase.com/institute/all-topics/household-financial-health/drawing-on-investment-wealth-full-report "Report") shows. And although older and richer people are leading the rise, withdrawals have increased across age and income groups, the researchers found, suggesting that “a growing portion of younger individuals are also using investment wealth to fund spending.”

Homeowners, who have seen the value of their houses surge over the past few years, are taking loans against those assets to finance large expenses. Loans against a home’s equity, known as HELOCs, rose 9.4% to the highest level since 2017 in the second quarter from the same period last year, according to Fed data.

Historically, a large share of HELOCs are used for home projects, according to equity analysts at Jefferies. With 30-year mortgage rates now above 7%, those who locked in at a much lower rate are likely to continue spending heavily on their homes.

Meanwhile lower-income families are resorting to personal debt. A recent [poll](https://state.nokidhungry.org/texas/2026/09/23/half-of-parents-in-texas-are-skipping-meals-to-afford-enough-groceries-for-their-household/ "Click to view webpage.") commissioned by No Kid Hungry Texas found that 39% of parents in the country’s second-most populous state are taking on debt in order to pay for groceries.

Demand for loans this year has surprised Jessica Grostic, president and chief executive of Copper Basin Federal Credit Union, which serves four counties tucked into the Blue Ridge Mountains of Tennessee and Georgia. May and June were record-breaking months for the credit union and September, typically a slower month, was already surpassing expectations by the 25th.

Grostic says there’s been an uptick in people using a loan program that, based on direct deposit history, automatically lends customers up to $2,000.

“People are just sometimes desperate for cash to actually pay their bills, which is a scary place,” Grostic said. “Sometimes it all comes crashing down. I just don’t know when.”

kept.heading: YOU AUTOMATED YOUR BUILD. YOUR GROWTH IS STILL MANUAL (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Growth compounds when each marketing activity creates inputs for the next one. The author focuses on 3 growth loops: app installs can improve store visibility, content can inform the next post, and product usage can generate reviews and user content. The content loop is often the slowest because it requires the most manual work, yet it can have significant results. Find the slowest step in each loop and remove unnecessary manual handoffs so each cycle happens faster.
kept.article_text:
Title: You automated your build. Your growth is still manual. — Expo blog

URL Source: https://expo.dev/blog/you-automated-your-build-your-growth-is-still-manual

Markdown Content:
_Mike Khristo is CEO and co-founder of [Layers](https://layers.com/)._

…

In July [Liam Du wrote here about taking Wellspoken from 400 users to hundreds of thousands of downloads](https://expo.dev/blog/how-to-grow-usage-and-revenue-for-your-mobile-app). At the end he lists what he learned, and the first lesson is that growth is a portfolio: no single channel got him there, several smaller wins stacked up.

That's true. I'd add one thing to it.

Read his story again and the components are wired together. Retention and engagement lift his App Store ranking, the ranking brings installs, and those installs produce the signals that lift the ranking again. His UGC operation finds a format that converts, the converted users leave reviews, and the reviews make the next batch of content convert better.

Every output is feeding an input. That's a loop, and he built a good one.

Most people run the same components as a checklist. The distance between those two things is most of the gap between apps that compound and apps that plateau.

A funnel is a sequence with an exit at the bottom. Traffic arrives, a fraction converts, and the only way to get more out is to put more in at the top. Every gain is linear and every gain is bought.

A loop routes its own output back to its own input. Users generate something (retention data, reviews, content, referrals) that makes the next cycle cheaper than the last one. The compounding is structural.

You already think this way. Your CI pipeline is a loop: a commit triggers a build, the build runs tests, the tests gate the deploy, the deploy produces telemetry, the telemetry shapes the next commit. Nobody would run those five stages as separate manual jobs with a person carrying artifacts between them. But that is how most apps run growth.

**The store loop.** Installs create behavioral signals that can help the stores understand which results are useful, while ratings, reviews and app quality can also affect discovery. Better visibility can then produce more installs. The interesting recent change is semantic relevance. In February 2026, Apple published research on an LLM-assisted App Store ranker that balances behavioral signals with how well an app actually matches a search. Its largest gains were on tail queries, where there's less historical behavior to learn from.

For a new app, that strengthens the case for targeting specific, semantically clear searches rather than relying only on broad category terms. Cycle time: weeks.

**The content loop.** You build something, capture it, post it, see what lands, make more of what landed. In a dataset of 23 million short-form videos, a follow-up on the same topic at the same length after a hit earned roughly 36% more views than switching subjects. The window is generous at first, so two hours later and four days later perform about the same, then it shuts after about a week. Cycle time: days.

**The proof loop.** Usage generates reviews and user content, that social proof raises conversion, and the higher conversion brings more usage. Liam's point about review prompts is the right one: the prompt harvests sentiment about the product already created. The loop only runs if the product earns it. Cycle time: continuous.

Notice the pattern. The content loop has the shortest natural cycle time of the three, and for most solo developers it's the one running slowest, because it's the most manual.

**Latency.** A loop compounds at the rate it completes cycles. If you need two weeks to work out what performed, the context that made it perform has already moved. This is why the sequel window matters: the advantage is real and it expires. A winning post is evidence about a moment. Platforms tell you what worked and none of them tell you why.

**Handoffs.** Every point where a human copies context from one tool into another is a place the loop stalls. Keyword research lives in one place, content in another, scheduling in a third, ad platforms in a fourth, analytics in a fifth. The connective tissue is you, at 11pm, pasting things between tabs. Liam solved this with dozens of creators and a campaign manager, which works and is completely out of reach for most people reading this.

This is the part where the parallel to Expo is hard to miss.

Ten years ago, shipping cross-platform meant maintaining a toolchain: the right Xcode on the right machine, signing, submission, a separate "everything" for Android. Most of that work was connective tissue, and the connective tissue was a person. EAS collapsed it. A solo developer can now run an app at hundreds of thousands of users without opening Xcode because the steps between commit and store stopped needing someone in the middle.

The growth stack sits roughly where the build stack was. Same shape of problem, same disconnected steps, same person in the middle. We started Layers to close those handoffs, and one belief drives the design: generative systems are only as good as the structured context they get before they generate. Brand guidelines and a URL are thin context. Your codebase, your store listing and your usage data are thick context, and they're already sitting there.

That's the product argument and I'll leave it there. The useful part holds regardless of what you use: optimize for cycle time and number of handoffs.

**Draw your loop.** Four or five nodes, arrows showing what feeds what. Most people find they have a funnel with a hopeful arrow at the end.

**Time each leg.** How long from shipping a feature to content about it going live? From a post landing to a follow-up? From a retention gain to seeing it in your ranking? The slowest leg sets your compounding rate.

**Remove one human handoff.** Pick the leg with the worst ratio of time spent to judgment required. That's almost always a copy-paste step, and it's usually the one blocking the content loop.

**Feed it something you're currently throwing away.** Every app produces raw material continuously and most of it gets used once and deleted. Your changelog is content. Your support inbox holds the exact words people use to describe the problem, which is where your store copy and your keywords should come from. Generated output can carry the volume. The raw material has to come from you, and it's most useful the week it appears.

The loop is already there. The question is how fast it turns.

kept.heading: WE VIBE CODED OUR OWN CALENDLY. OUR AI AGENT PUSHED US TO DO IT, AND IT WAS RIGHT (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: A 3-person team built its own scheduling tool in 20 mins after its AI agent identified a limitation with Calendly. The custom booker connects scheduling to Salesforce and prospect data, showing each prospect a personalized prospectus and routing them to the right salesperson based on account ownership. The team could have integrated Calendly, but the agent determined that most of the custom logic would still need to be built. The default remains buying software, with custom builds reserved for narrow workflows where proprietary data creates an advantage.

# We Vibe Coded Our Own Calendly. Our AI Agent Pushed Us To Do It, and It Was Right.

by [Jason Lemkin](https://www.saastr.com/author/jasonlkn/ "Posts by Jason Lemkin") | [Blog Posts](https://www.saastr.com/category/resource-type/blog-posts/)

Calendly is cheap, proven, and works well. We used it for years, and a three-person team has little reason to build its own scheduling tool.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_4ArZ5j6tkA)

We built one anyway. Our agent built it on Replit in about 20 minutes, and it now sits at the end of our sponsor sales funnel. We had two reasons, and the first one wouldn’t have been enough by itself.

## Reason #1: 10K Recommended It and Offered to Build It Himself

10K is our AI VP of Marketing, and increasingly our AI VP of Revenue. He runs on Replit, writes to Salesforce, runs our ad campaigns, handles quote-to-cash, and is connected to about 30 other systems.

When Amelia and 10K were rebuilding our inbound sponsor flow, 10K suggested we stop using Calendly and build our own booker. He offered to build it himself.

An agent wanting to build something is a bad reason to build it. Agents like to build, and following every suggestion would leave us maintaining a dozen homegrown tools we don’t need. But the suggestion was worth asking 10K to justify, so we asked him why.

## Reason #2: The Booker Does Something Calendly Couldn’t

Before this, David sent prospects his Calendly link and Amelia sent her Read AI link. Neither tool was connected to anything else we run.

10K and Amelia were building a flow where a sponsor prospect books a time and gets two more things at the same moment:

1.   **A custom, real-time prospectus.** It has their company name, their competitors who were at SaaStr AI Annual, and the packages the agent recommends for them. It’s a tokenized page on our site, so the link they already have updates as we learn more about them.
2.   **A meeting with the right person on our team.** The agent routes based on which sponsors each of us already works with. When Base44 came in, it went to Amelia instead of David, because Amelia owns Replit and Lovable and the agent weighted that volume over David owning Vercel.

The booking link also carries the company name and connects back to the prospectus they were reading. If someone opens the booker and leaves without booking, 10K tells Amelia and offers to draft the follow-up email.

Calendly has no way to know who owns which sponsor accounts, what’s in a prospect’s custom prospectus, or what the heat map showed them reading. That data lives in 10K and Salesforce.

## Why 10K Said Build Instead of Integrate

We could have kept Calendly and connected it through their API. 10K’s view was that building the whole booker would be easier than doing part of it in Calendly and wiring the routing, prospectus delivery, and bounce tracking around it.

The routing and the prospectus both depend on our own data, so we would have built most of the logic ourselves either way, plus maintained an integration with Calendly on top.

The build took 20 minutes. Before it, the calendar was the one step in the funnel where we couldn’t see what a prospect did. Now we can.

## Amelia’s First Reaction Was “It’s Just a Calendar”

A standalone calendar isn’t worth building, and Amelia said so. What justified this one was everything it connects to: by the time a prospect books, the system already knows who they are, what they read, and which of us should take the call.

At 20 minutes of agent time, the bar was low. If 10K had estimated two weeks, we would have kept Calendly.

## We Still Buy Almost Everything

Salesforce, Qualified, Clay, ZoomInfo, Artisan, Monaco, Gamma, and Clarity are all bought, and we tell founders to buy by default.

When we do build, it’s usually a narrow piece. Zapier was silently losing about 20% of our signups before they reached Salesforce. We kept Zapier for the authenticated triggers, which are tedious to rebuild and weren’t causing problems, and moved the action steps into our own code, since that’s where the signups were getting lost.

The booker was a similar call. Scheduling itself is fine to rent. Deciding who a prospect meets and what they see when they book required data no scheduling vendor has.

## The Questions We Ask When 10K Wants to Build

10K makes vendor decisions quickly. It picked Microsoft Clarity for heat mapping without evaluating alternatives. It also dropped a vendor its own agent had shortlisted within 12 hours, after running the pricing. Its calls are often good, and we still check them.

When it proposes a build, we have it answer these first:

*   **What does this do that the vendor can’t?** If it does the same thing more cheaply, we buy.
*   **Would an API integration cover most of it?** If so, we integrate.
*   **What data does it need that only we have?** On the booker, this was the deciding answer.
*   **How long will it take, and what happens if it breaks?** Twenty minutes, with a Calendly link as the fallback, made this an easy yes.

For any sensitive workflow, we also ask an agent what it plans to do before it does it. We did that here too.

## 10K’s Biggest Contributions Now Are Product Ideas

A year ago 10K was suggesting things like a referral program for tickets. Now most of its value comes from product recommendations. The tokenized prospectus for inbound was its idea: it looked at what we’d built for renewals and pointed out that we already had most of the pieces. The booker was its idea. Its current proposal is a version of itself for David and the sales team, since David doesn’t have the backend access Amelia has.

We still default to buying. When an agent pushes you to build instead, ask it why and push back.

It may have a great idea.

kept.article_text:
Title: Building advertising for the way people use AI

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/rYcBcI

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing a new visual ad format in ChatGPT, expanding our measurement tools and partnerships, and developing new ways to understand brand suitability.

ChatGPT reaches 1.2 billion people each week, making it the world’s largest AI-native consumer platform. Advertising helps us bring the benefits of AI to more people. That broad access is central to our mission, and a strength of our business. It allows us to serve a much larger market than subscriptions alone, while giving businesses a new way to reach people as they explore ideas, make decisions and discover products and services relevant to what they’re trying to accomplish.

## Bringing products and services to life

Our new visual ad format helps people imagine how products and services could fit into their lives. Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy. For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.

Initially, we’ll test this new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT for users on the Free and Go plans. Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created. As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Testing will begin later this month in the US with an initial group of advertisers.

## Measuring the impact of ChatGPT Ads

Our measurement philosophy for ChatGPT Ads is focused on supporting both in-house and partner-led measurement solutions. Today, we’re expanding our measurement tools and partner ecosystem to help advertisers understand how ChatGPT Ads contribute to their business using the systems they already rely on.

Integrations with Hightouch, Tealium, and LiveRamp make it easier for advertisers to send conversion data from their existing systems to ChatGPT Ads.

We now support leading attribution partners across the web and app space, enabling Conversions API, reporting, and click attribution solutions with companies including AppsFlyer, Triple Whale, Adjust, DV Rockerbox, Northbeam, Branch, Singular, Kochava, Airbridge, and Tenjin. We also have partnerships with full-funnel and advanced measurement partners, including Fospha, Measured, and INCRMNTAL.

Incrementality measurement plays an important role in building a fuller understanding of advertising’s business impact. While our work on incrementality is still in its early stages, we’re partnering with Haus, Measured, and WorkMagic to explore geo-based experiments to help advertisers understand the causal impact of ChatGPT Ads.

Early partner findings illustrate strong performance across different measurement approaches. According to DV Rockerbox, WeightWatchers’ attributed cost per acquisition on ChatGPT Ads was 15.3% lower than its blended paid-search benchmark. WorkMagic reported statistically significant lift for wellness brand Dose, with 67% of incremental purchases coming from net-new customers. And according to Triple Whale, 93% of Portland Leather’s visitors from ChatGPT Ads were new.

Read more about these measurement tools and partnerships on our Ads Blog [here⁠(opens in a new window)](http://ads.openai.com/blog/more-ways-to-measure).

## Building confidence in alignment with our Ads Principles

Confidence in advertising also depends on understanding the environment where ads can appear. OpenAI’s [advertising policies](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/policies/ad-policies/) and guardrails are designed to protect users, preserve trust, and give brands confidence in their ad placements. Our placement guardrails assess whether a conversation is appropriate for advertising, helping keep ads out of emotionally vulnerable, sensitive, or otherwise unsuitable contexts.

Automated review, human oversight, and ongoing monitoring help us identify and address policy violations and improve our safeguards over time. For narrow placement requirements specific to a brand’s own policies, Negative Phrases are now available to qualifying advertisers.

We’re also developing brand suitability evaluation pilots with DoubleVerify (DV) and Integral Ad Science (IAS) to help advertisers build a better understanding of the ads environment. This approach allows independent partners to assess how our brand safety standards are applied in a controlled testing environment, without accessing private user conversations. Our goal is to give advertisers greater transparency into how those safeguards work while protecting conversation privacy.

## Expanding the features of ChatGPT Ads

Our new visual ad format helps people discover products and services and imagine how they could fit into their lives, while giving advertisers new ways to tell their stories more visually. Across ChatGPT Ads, expanded measurement and brand suitability efforts help businesses understand campaign impact and build confidence in the contexts where their ads appear. These features are consistent with our ads principles: ChatGPT’s answers stay independent, conversations stay private, and users remain in control of their experience.

Today’s updates are part of our broader ambition to help people discover products and services, evaluate options, and make decisions in ChatGPT. We will continue to evolve our ad platform with new formats and capabilities to help businesses reach customers in useful and relevant ways and provide opportunities for businesses of all sizes to grow and thrive.

Businesses can sign up today for ads at [ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a new window)](http://ads.openai.com/)⁠⁠.

kept.heading: PREDICTION: THE NEXT MASSIVE GOOGLE UPDATE IS AROUND THE CORNER (16 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google tends to rewrite its documentation shortly before a major update, and it has just rewritten its guidance on AI content and authorship. Publishing AI text at scale without manual review now counts as little to no effort, and invented authors with AI headshots count as deception. The GEO tactics built to win AI answers, including self-ranking listicles and paid mentions, repeat old SEO spam patterns that Google has historically shut down. Cutting or consolidating scaled content before an update is often easier than recovering after one.

Title: Prediction: the next massive Google update is around the corner

URL Source: https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/prediction-the-next-massive-google

Published Time: 2026-10-04T20:22:46+00:00

Markdown Content:
If you work in SEO long enough, you start to notice that things tend to move in cycles. First: SEOs (and now GEOs) find a way to influence the organic or AI results or exploit Google’s ranking systems to gain visibility. Their tactics become popularized, shared widely, and duplicated all over the world. Then the search engine (and now AI companies) build systems to stop those tactics from working.

[I’ve presented on this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nw-dllribgQ)- what I call the cycle of SEO - [many times](https://ipullrank.com/seo-week-2025-lily-ray), because I’ve made it my mission to warn companies to help them avoid making the same mistakes as the businesses that come to me after they’ve been burned by Google. Once you’ve worked with enough affected companies and seen firsthand the devastation that these updates can cause, warning people starts to feel like a personal responsibility. Nobody should have to go through years of lost visibility and revenue because of a tactic someone sold them as a growth hack - especially companies that don’t even know that the tactics they (or their SEO agencies) are using are against Google’s guidelines.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gF5V!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3238934c-44d6-4328-b21c-6da7b759e4e2_989x607.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gF5V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3238934c-44d6-4328-b21c-6da7b759e4e2_989x607.png)

The visual representation of the “Cycle of SEO” that I’ve used across various conference presentations in 2025 and 2026

There have been very few popular SEO exploits that Google didn’t eventually smack down - or at least try to. Google’s crackdowns aren’t perfect, and some loopholes always slip through. But some of the biggest updates in Google’s history - Florida, Panda, Penguin, the 2018 Medic update, the Helpful Content Update, and the March 2024 core update - all taught the same lesson: you do NOT want to be on the wrong side when Google finally decides to take action.

These updates can be brutal and far-reaching. In my years working on website recovery, I’ve seen dozens of sites that only dipped a toe into “gray area” tactics get hit almost as hard as pure spam sites. With whatever SEO (and now GEO) trend is currently working to trick Google’s systems, it’s usually not a question of if Google will respond, but when.

If you’ve experienced this cycle before, it should be pretty clear where in it we are right now. In this post, I’ll explain why I and several other people who focus on algorithm updates are predicting that another huge update is coming.

*   **In my experience, Google updates its documentation with clues before launching major updates.**

*   **Google rewrote its guidance on AI content this week.** It now says it’s “critical” to manually fact-check and review all AI-generated content before publishing, including titles, meta descriptions, structured data, and alt text.

*   **Google added new language to its helpful content guidelines** defining “main content” and the 4 things quality raters look for: effort, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy. Mass-producing AI content without oversight is now named as an example of little to no effort. _(This also happens to be the single biggest culprit behind sites I’ve seen get hit by algorithm updates this year.)_

*   **Google now calls fake authors a form of deception.** AI-generated headshots, made-up names, and false credentials are named explicitly as a signal of a low-quality page.

*   **Google’s own people are saying it out loud.** At Search Central Live in Barcelona this week, Gary Illyes said [scaled content is becoming more of a problem than link spam](https://weareroast.com/news/google-search-central-live-deep-dive-barcelona-day-3-recap/).

*   According to [my research](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/why-calling-yourself-the-best-could), Google appears to have already started reducing the efficacy of publishing self-promotional listicles in AI Overviews.

*   **Multiple companies are openly selling paid mentions and listicle placements to influence AI answers, usually with no mention of nofollow, sponsored labels, or disclosure.** When those placements include links that pass ranking credit, that’s a violation of Google’s [link spam policy](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies#link-spam), and Google has already said seeking inauthentic mentions isn’t as helpful as it might seem.

*   **Google has released 4 spam updates in 2026** (March, June, August, and September), compared to just one in all of 2025. The time between them keeps shrinking.

*   **Other people who study algorithm updates are seeing the same thing**, including [Glenn Gabe](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/i/218673481/glenn-gabe), [Marie Haynes](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/i/218673481/marie-haynes), and [Cyrus Shepard](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/i/218673481/cyrus-shepard).

*   **I’ve spent this year working with companies that were already hit by Google in 2026**, both algorithmically and with manual actions, and the patterns are clear.

I remember the night before the March 2024 core update well. [Marie Haynes](https://www.mariehaynes.com/) - who has specialized in algorithm updates, manual actions, and website recovery even longer than I have - and I were sitting at a bar in Vegas before our talks that week at Pubcon. My presentation would be about the tactics I saw sites using that I predicted were likely to get hit hard by the next Google update.

I told Marie I was confident Google would _eventually_ do something, but I was also surprised it was taking so long to go after what seemed like such obvious examples of spam in its results. She told me she had a feeling Google was going to drop something really big, really soon.

She wasn’t wrong. The next day, [Google announced the March 2024 core update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies) - which ended up being one of the biggest updates in Google’s history, and [at 45 days](https://status.search.google.com/incidents/1jW2F89qC2NxJBWGiKxE), the longest core update rollout Google has on record - along with 3 new spam policies: [site reputation abuse](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies#site-reputation), [scaled content abuse](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies#scaled-content), and [expired domain abuse](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies#expired-domains). I spent the evening rewriting my slides. These tactics were no longer just “likely” to put a site at risk - Google had named specific policies targeting the same tactics I was about to present in [my talk](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/fear-and-loathing-google-in-las-vegas-lily-ray-seo-presentation-2024/266662509#11).

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cz3p!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F693a3491-f0fc-465d-836a-be81c6e5917b_760x418.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cz3p!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F693a3491-f0fc-465d-836a-be81c6e5917b_760x418.png)

A slide from my March 2024 Pubcon presentation, listing the spam tactics likely to be hit by Google’s upcoming updates

Looking back, the warning signs were everywhere:

*   **Google told us to “buckle up.”** At BrightonSEO San Diego in November 2023, Google’s Search Liaison at the time, Danny Sullivan, said there were so many ranking improvements coming that he didn’t want to say “buckle up,” because people would freak out ([recording via Search Engine Roundtable](https://www.seroundtable.com/google-buckle-up-comment-37380.html)). The phrase stuck anyway, and Google [repeated the message in January and again in February](https://searchengineland.com/google-released-massive-search-quality-improvements-with-march-2024-core-update-and-multiple-spam-updates-438144).

*   **The Search Liaison account kept hinting at something big.** Danny [replied to people on X](https://twitter.com/searchliaison/status/1733190735745466819)[for months](https://twitter.com/searchliaison/status/1744295345834643734), implying that the specific spam problems they flagged were being worked on.

*   **Google quietly changed its stance on AI content.** With the [September 2023 Helpful Content Update](https://searchengineland.com/google-september-2023-helpful-content-system-update-rolling-out-431978), Google removed the words “written by people” from its guidance and replaced them with “helpful content created for people.” From what I saw, many people interpreted this as a green light for scaling AI content. Six months later came the scaled content abuse policy.

*   **It was not a secret that Google’s SEO spam problem was out of control.** In November 2023, The Verge published [“The people who ruined the internet,”](https://www.theverge.com/features/23931789/seo-search-engine-optimization-experts-google-results) a long feature blaming SEOs for the state of search. (I was interviewed and quoted in this article in the months leading up to its publication, right around the time of the Helpful Content Update.)

    *   Back in 2022, Charlie Warzel at The Atlantic had already [asked whether Google search was dying](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2022/06/google-search-algorithm-internet/661325/), in an article that also went viral.

When Google finally took action, it came in the form of a massive core update, along with 3 new spam policies that led to manual actions against companies of all sizes. Google said the update reduced low-quality, unoriginal content in its results [by 45%](https://blog.google/products/search/google-search-update-march-2024/).

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!amS9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10b792fd-5ad3-4397-8585-3c6d332a7a34_1326x483.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!amS9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10b792fd-5ad3-4397-8585-3c6d332a7a34_1326x483.png)

The impact of the March 2024 core update on 5 sites (letter A), via Sistrix Visibility Index

The warning signs before the March 2024 update weren’t unusual. Many of Google’s biggest crackdowns were preceded by public warnings that were not always taken seriously. And from what I have observed, Google often updates its documentation or quality rater guidelines shortly before - or right alongside - major updates. If you know where to look, the clues are usually there in writing.

*   **January 2011:** Matt Cutts [wrote that spam had increased](https://techcrunch.com/2011/01/21/google-spam-really-has-increased-lately-were-fixing-that-and-content-farms-are-next/) and that people were asking for stronger action on content farms. **What followed:** the Panda update, February 2011.

*   **March 2012:** Matt Cutts [said at SXSW](https://outspokenmedia.com/seo/over-optimization-penalty) that Google was working on a penalty for “over-optimized” sites. **What followed:** the Penguin update, April 2012.

*   **July 20, 2018:** The quality rater guidelines added new emphasis on [the reputation of a site and its content creators](https://www.rebelmouse.com/google-algorithm-updates-2018). **What followed: the “Medic”** core update on August 1, 2018 - 12 days later.

*   **September to November 2023:** Google removed “written by people” from its helpful content guidance, and Danny Sullivan said “buckle up.” **What followed: the September** 2023 Helpful Content Update, then the March 2024 core update and 3 new spam policies.

*   **January 23, 2025:** The quality rater guidelines [rewrote the Lowest and Low quality sections](https://searchengineland.com/google-updates-search-quality-raters-guidelines-with-a-focus-on-spam-451073) to match the spam policies, adding [scaled content abuse and AI content published without human review](https://www.seozoom.com/?p=27852). **What followed: the March 2025**[core update](https://ppc.land/google-releases-march-2025-core-update/) on March 13 - 7 weeks later.

*   **May 15, 2026:** Google [clarified](https://developers.google.com/search/updates) that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode, and published a new guide on optimizing for AI features. **What followed: the May 2026** core update on May 21 - 6 days later - followed by the June 2026 spam update the next month.

*   **September to October 2026:** Google rewrote its AI content, main content, and authorship guidance, and Google speakers said scaled content is a bigger problem than link spam. **I think by this point, it’s fair to assume from these recent communications that something big is on the horizon.**

The gap between the warning and the update has ranged from a few weeks to a few months. In some cases, the timeline can be much shorter: Google even [announced the Helpful Content Update a week before it started rolling out](https://blog.google/products/search/more-content-by-people-for-people-in-search/) in August 2022.

On October 1, Google updated its [guidance on using generative AI content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content). It now reads:

> “It is critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing.”

The same review applies to titles, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text. As Barry Schwartz [pointed out](https://www.seroundtable.com/google-updates-ai-content-guidelines-factcheck-review-42217.html), “critical” is a word Google rarely uses in its documentation. The page also now points readers to the sections of the quality rater guidelines on scaled content abuse and on content made with little to no effort or originality.

I see this as the biggest warning sign, because scaled AI content is also the biggest culprit behind the algorithmic demotions and penalties I’ve seen this year. This content is often full of hallucinations and inaccuracies. Not only does this create a poor experience for Google’s users, but it’s also a problem for Google’s own AI systems, which can pick up those errors and repeat them back to users as fact in products like AI Overviews and AI Mode. I wrote about this cycle in [“The AI Slop Loop.](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/the-ai-slop-loop)”

This same week, Google added a new section to [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), the document I’ve long considered the clearest explanation of what Google’s systems are trying to reward. It says the quality of the main content is “one of the most critical factors” for assessing page quality, and lists 4 things raters are trained to look for: **effort**, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy.

The definition of effort is the part that should worry anyone scaling content with AI:

> “...using generative AI to produce large amounts of text without manual oversight or curation **represents little to no effort.**”

The accuracy bar is also higher for YMYL topics, where content “must be highly accurate and consistent with established expert consensus.”

If you use AI to create or help create content, especially at scale, I would take this as a serious warning from Google. In my experience, many companies assume _their_ AI content is safe, or better than the content Google is warning about. But almost every company that has come to me after being hit by an algorithm update thought its content was better than Google ultimately decided it was.

Google also added this to the same page:

> “Fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names, or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception. Any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy to both users and our automated quality systems, and is a signal of a low-quality page.”

The quality rater guidelines already told raters to treat fake author profiles as deception. This is something I’ve [written, posted, and presented about for years](https://x.com/lilyraynyc/status/1716837784454062181), and it’s certainly not a new tactic. What’s new is that Google is now saying it directly to site owners, and connecting it to its automated systems rather than just to raters. [Search Engine Journal found](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-fake-author-warning-site-owner-guidance/591806/) this paragraph wasn’t on the page in June.

This isn’t a theoretical problem - it’s already causing quality issues in Google’s results. Fake AI experts have been showing up everywhere - including an AI-generated “art therapist” who was [quoted more than 30 times in the media](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/prominent-art-therapist-quoted-by-vice-forbes-and-others-is-ai-generated/) before anyone noticed. I also observed this as a common tactic [employed by sites hit by the Helpful Content Update](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/the-helpful-content-update-everything-you-need-to-know/287230579#39) and other recent core updates, including in 2026.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Dqoq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2262b9ef-227a-4704-86d1-e980a6f27eeb_756x417.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Dqoq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2262b9ef-227a-4704-86d1-e980a6f27eeb_756x417.png)

A slide from my 2023 presentation about the Helpful Content Update, listing “Fake Authors” as a commonly abused tactic among impacted websites

At [Search Central Live in Barcelona](https://weareroast.com/news/google-search-central-live-deep-dive-barcelona-day-3-recap/) this week, according to John Campbell’s recap:

*   Gary Illyes said scaled content is now becoming more of a problem than link spam (!!!)

*   Duy Nguyen said there have been more spam updates recently because there is so much more new content, and that the team is now using AI to catch more of it.

*   Duy also told the room to read the quality rater guidelines, and defined quality using the same 4 attributes from the new documentation: effort, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy.

[Google said it updated](https://developers.google.com/search/updates) its AI content documentation “to get our documentation in sync with our presentations we use at our developer events.” In other words, the message Google has been giving in person is now in writing.

From my perspective, Google puts this guidance in writing so that when an update hits and site owners are caught off guard, it can point back to the documentation and show that the warnings were there all along.

Many of the most popular GEO tactics right now are old SEO spam tactics with a new label: mass-produced AI content, self-promotional listicles where a brand ranks itself #1, fake reviews and [“inauthentic mentions”](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide#mythbusting) bought to influence what AI tools recommend, and automated Reddit posting.

While these approaches have undoubtedly worked well to influence AI responses and citations so far, [some of this is already being cleaned up](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/is-google-finally-cracking-down-on). In my research on self-promotional listicles cited in AI Overviews, [the brand that ranked itself #1 was left out of the actual recommendation 69% of the time](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/why-calling-yourself-the-best-could). I recently updated this data, looking at 100 “best B2B software” queries, and found that this trend has grown even stronger in September 2026:

Compared to June, Google’s AI Overviews now cite 38% fewer self-promotional “best of” listicles, and they leave the publishing brand out of the recommendation 83% of the time**, up from 69% in June.**

Also, in 70% of cases, the listicle is now helping competitors get recommended while the brand that published it is left out**:**

[![Image 5: Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!I9fV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fddd74945-dec4-4846-965b-1c03029b0660_787x269.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!I9fV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fddd74945-dec4-4846-965b-1c03029b0660_787x269.png)

It’s not just Google that’s taking action against spam. In March, Reddit started [labeling legitimate bot accounts and requiring some suspicious accounts to verify they’re human](https://www.techspot.com/news/111836-reddit-cracks-down-bots-new-labels-human-verification.html). In July, it [said its automated systems were catching 25,000 spammy posts and comments a day](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-06/reddit-is-cracking-down-on-ai-marketing-slop-with-its-own-ai), as it works to stop brands from planting posts meant to get them recommended by ChatGPT and Gemini. Reddit also recently banned[4 subreddits](https://otterly.ai/blog/reddit-ban-geo-experiment/) used in a GEO experiment that relied on automation bots for upvotes and comments.

Paid brand mentions - which are basically the 2026 version of paid link building, but focused on generative AI responses - deserve their own warning. A growing number of companies now openly sell placements on other people’s sites, pitched as a way to get recommended by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and AI Overviews. Here’s what’s being sold right now:

*   Placements in third-party “best X” and “top X” listicles, sold per placement and priced by the site’s Domain Rating or Domain Authority, often starting around $135 to $250 each.

*   Packages of “AI brand mentions” added to existing listicles, reviews, and buying guides, such as 5 mentions for $1,500.

*   Listicle placements that guarantee a dofollow link.

*   Agency playbooks that say that if outreach doesn’t work, “many of these sites accept paid placements” - sometimes for a one-time payment of $100 or $200.

*   Fully managed “offsite” services from AI visibility platforms that handle publisher outreach, content, negotiation, and payment to land mentions on third-party sites.

*   Integrations that send the sites AI tools cite to a placement network, which automatically handles outreach, drafting, negotiations, and payment, offering either fixed-price placements or “reverse mentions.”

When these placements include links that pass ranking credit, this is link buying with a new name. Google’s [link spam policy](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies#link-spam) lists “exchanging money for links, or posts that contain links” as a violation. Paid links are only allowed when they’re [qualified](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links) with rel=“sponsored” or rel=“nofollow,” and the [FTC](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255/section-255.5) generally requires paid relationships behind endorsements to be clearly disclosed - something these sales pages rarely mention. kept.heading: I SHOPPED FOR SOCCER SHOES WITH CHATGPT, CLAUDE, AND MUSE. ONE GOT ME CLOSER TO BUYING (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI shopping assistants need to balance choice with guidance to build purchase confidence. ChatGPT won by showing 3 soccer shoe options with a recommended pick and clear comparison. Claude offered useful product details but lacked images and purchase links. Muse made shopping more engaging with interactive questions and visuals but recommended the wrong shoes. The test suggests giving shoppers a few options plus a clear recommendation can make AI-assisted purchases easier.
kept.article_text:
Title: I shopped for soccer shoes with ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse. One got me closer to buying.

URL Source: https://kristenberman.substack.com/p/i-shopped-for-soccer-shoes-with-chatgpt

Published Time: 2026-10-01T20:42:32+00:00

Markdown Content:
**🎬****Every week I share a short (fun!) product video teardown and some hot takes on behavior change.****Pro tip: The video only takes 〜5 minutes at 2x speed. And it will be more memorable. ;) ⏩**

A confession before we start: I mispronounce Muse for the entire video, with total confidence. I’m in good company, at least: the U.S. Secretary of Education once [called AI “A1”](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/xsRUk0dMJu4) (like the steak sauce) while talking about AI in schools.

I needed new indoor soccer shoes, so I asked Claude, ChatGPT, and Muse to help me buy a pair. Then I scored them the way a behavioral scientist shops: how they set up the decision, how they frame the options, and whether they give me anything to compare against.

When a product recommends something, it’s tempting to think the fastest path to a sale is a single right answer: ask a few questions, narrow it down, hand over the pick. That’s roughly what Claude did. Once I told it my budget was $100, it went from four well-described shoes to one. ChatGPT, in text chat, narrowed to one Adidas shoe in two colors with no explanation. There’s no world where I buy a $100 shoe from that.

At the point of decision, the question in my head is “is this actually right for me?” A single option gives me nothing to check it against, and people struggle to judge things in isolation. Seeing a few options, including why some of them aren’t right for me, makes me more likely to believe the one that is.

**Chat GPT won the choice architecture.** It gave me three options, brand, price and a link. It named a “starting pick.” Having choices plus guidance telling me where to start made me feel a lot more comfortable.

**Claude treated this like a big decision.** Claude’s descriptions were the best of the three (”good for wide feet” is the kind of detail that makes a purchase feel safe), but without prices or pictures it was hard to get excited about any of them.

**Muse most reflected a fun shopping experience.**The questions feel like a game, it shows you how it’s thinking, and it shows pictures, which the others didn’t. This felt the most like actual shopping.

So who won? In my experience, ChatGPT’s chart was the clearest decision frame: three options and one recommendation. Muse took itself out of the game by recommending the wrong shoes up front and it will likely need to improve on the browsing experience to give me full confidence in the purchase. And Claude’s detail was nailing it, it just didn’t deliver the full shopping experience (like a link to buy!).

Any product that recommends something is designing a decision frame, and that frame’s job is to make people confident in the answer. Too many choices and people can’t make a decision, and too few choices and they won’t trust it. Same goes for information and context about the item. If there isn’t enough information to drive confidence, then the user will delay their decision and bounce.

There is no one right answer to choice architecture (I wish there was). But we do have some leads on what you could try first. Here are two case studies that worked. Both times we gave people three options with a recommended version.

*   We offered new employees in [Intuit’s payroll onboarding](https://irrationallabs.com/case-studies/intuit-payroll-how-we-increased-emergency-savings-by-5x/) three paycheck savings amounts with a recommended middle option. Around 20% saved, against 3% in the control, and most people took the recommended middle: it told them where to start, and the alternatives gave them a reason to trust it.

*   For [B3, Brazil’s stock exchange](https://irrationallabs.com/case-studies/simpler-choices-how-we-drove-5x-more-reinvestment-in-brazilian-treasury-bonds/), we emailed investors with maturing Treasury bonds three options similar to the bond they already held. Each was labeled by length of time so people could match it to their goals, and the most popular one was flagged. That version drove about 4.3x more scheduled reinvestments than the control.

These are small moves, and they may not all fit your product, so test them. In the video, I grade all three on a behavioral science scorecard, make a bet on who’s ahead in ecommerce, and get into why every AI assistant wants you to check out without leaving the chat.

If you’re working on an ecommerce experience or any kind of decision frame inside an LLM, I’d love to hear about it. And if you play soccer, I’d love to play with you! Email me at kristen@irrationallabs.com.
