kept.heading: THE ECONOMICS OF THE STREAK: LOYALTY PROGRAMS AND STARS (10 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Loyalty programs use loss aversion and goal gradients to make accumulated points feel like possessions worth protecting. A 100-day streak can become more motivating to preserve than the underlying habit, while being close to a reward or tier encourages extra spending. Programs also benefit from unredeemed points through breakage and collect purchase data. They can reward behaviors customers already value or drive spending and engagement mainly to avoid losing accumulated progress.
kept.article_text:
Title: The Economics of the Streak: Loyalty Programs and Stars

URL Source: https://destbreso.com/blog/bcs-the-economics-of-the-streak

Published Time: 2026-10-02T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
> **"Losses loom larger than gains."**_Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1979_

![Image 1: A fan of airline and store loyalty and rewards cards](https://destbreso.com/images/blog/behavioral-capture/loyalty-cards.jpg)

_Photo: [Mattes](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=603878), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons._

After all the slot machines and casinos of numbers, here is a capture system you can hold in your hand and feel good about. A coffee shop gives you a card: buy nine, the tenth is free. An app gives you a gold star for showing up. A language tool lights a little flame next to a number and asks you, gently, to come back tomorrow so the number can grow. An airline calls you Silver, then Gold, then Platinum, and means it as a compliment.

None of these feels like a slot machine. Nobody loses their savings to a stamp card. There is no jackpot, no random reward, no volatility, no ruin. These are the _gentlest_ machines in the entire series, and most of them are genuinely benign, even helpful. A streak that gets you to exercise, a points card that saves you money on things you would buy anyway: these can be small gifts.

And yet they are built from the same parts. The loyalty program is a behavioral capture system stripped down to its quietest essentials, running almost entirely on two mechanisms we have already met (loss aversion and the goal gradient) and one we have not named yet (the streak as an asset you cannot bear to lose). Studying the gentle case is illuminating _because_ it is gentle: with the jackpots and the volatility removed, you can see the underlying machinery with unusual clarity. Why can a 100-day streak become harder to break than the habit it was supposed to build? The answer is a small, exact piece of psychology, and once you see it in the friendly version you will recognize it everywhere.

* * *

### 1. The phenomenon

Watch what a streak does to you. The first few days of a daily-app streak mean little; if you miss day three, you shrug and start again. But somewhere around day 30, 50, 100, something shifts. The number itself becomes valuable, independent of the activity it tracks. You find yourself opening the app at 11:50pm, not because you want to do the thing, but because you cannot stand to lose the number. The streak has stopped being a record of your habit and become a possession you are protecting. People have paid for "streak freezes." People have done the bare-minimum token action, joylessly, for years, to keep a counter alive.

The same shift happens with status tiers. A traveler will book a worse, more expensive flight to keep their Gold status, and feel the loss of that status, if it lapses, as a genuine wound. A points-card holder will go out of their way, spend more, and choose a worse option to "not waste" the points they have accumulated. In every case the phenomenon is the same: an accumulated, displayed quantity (a streak, a tier, a points balance) becomes something you own, and owning it makes losing it hurt far more than gaining it ever pleased. That asymmetry is the whole machine.

* * *

### 2. The mathematical model

The engine is **loss aversion**: a loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equivalent gain feels good. Losing 50 dollars is not the mirror image of finding 50 dollars; it is about twice as painful. Kahneman and Tversky captured this in a "value function" that is steeper on the loss side than the gain side, and the multiplier (how much more losses hurt) is usually estimated around two. It is one of the most replicated findings in behavioral science and also, in recent years, one of the most argued about, with a strand of work holding that the asymmetry is weaker and more dependent on context than the textbook version suggests. The weaker version is enough for everything this post needs: in the situations these programs construct, giving something up reliably feels worse than never having had it.

Now apply it to a streak. When your streak is at zero, building it is a series of small _gains_, and gains are felt weakly. But once your streak is at 100, breaking it is a _loss_, and losses are felt about twice as strongly. So the streak quietly converts your daily decision from a weak "do I want the gain of continuing?" into a strong "can I bear the loss of breaking it?" The longer the streak, the bigger the thing you would lose, and the more the loss-aversion multiplier has to work with. The counter does not just record your behavior; it manufactures, day by day, a larger and larger potential loss that you must keep paying to avoid. That is why the 100-day streak holds you harder than the 3-day streak: not because the activity got more valuable, but because the _loss_ you are avoiding got bigger.

Layer on the **goal gradient** from the illusion-of-progress post (motivation rising as you approach a target, $M \left(\right. x \left.\right) \propto 1 / \left(\right. 1 - x \left.\right)$) and the tier system clicks into place too. "200 points from Gold" pulls hardest precisely when you are nearly there, so loyalty programs are designed to keep you always just short of the next tier, climbing the steep part of the curve, where a little more spending closes a gap that feels almost shut.

* * *

### The deep dive: prospect theory, the reference point, and why the streak is the trap

The reason a friendly counter can capture you is worth making precise, because it reveals that the trap is built not from the reward but from a _reference point_, and reference points can be installed.

Prospect theory describes how we value an outcome $x$ relative to a reference point, not in absolute terms. The value function looks roughly like

$$
v \left(\right. x \left.\right) = \left{\right. x^{\alpha} & x \geq 0 \left(\right. \text{gains} \left.\right) \\ - \lambda \textrm{ } \left(\right. - x \left.\right)^{\beta} & x < 0 \left(\right. \text{losses} \left.\right)
$$

with $\alpha , \beta \approx 0.88$ (we are slightly insensitive to magnitude) and, crucially, the **loss-aversion coefficient**$\lambda \approx 2.25$: the loss branch is steeper than the gain branch by that factor. Those particular numbers are the 1992 estimates from the cumulative version of the theory, not the 1979 paper that introduced it, and they are median fits to laboratory choices rather than constants of nature. Two features of this function do all the work.

First, **everything is measured from a reference point**, and the reference point is whatever you currently regard as the status quo. This is the lever. When you have a 100-day streak, your reference point silently becomes "I have a 100-day streak." Continuing merely _maintains_ the status quo (a near-zero gain, weakly felt), while breaking it is a _loss from the reference point_ (felt at the full $\lambda \approx 2.25$ multiplier). The asymmetry is not about the streak's objective worth; it is about which side of the reference point each choice falls on. The program's entire genius is moving your reference point upward as the streak grows, so that more and more of your possible futures are framed as losses, which loom large, rather than as foregone gains, which do not.

Second, the **endowment effect** (usually explained as a consequence of loss aversion) means we value things more once we own them, simply because giving them up registers as a loss. A streak, a tier, a points balance: the moment it is _yours_, parting with it triggers the steep loss branch. This is why "you'll lose your progress" is such a potent message and why programs display your accumulated status so prominently: the display is what makes it feel owned, and ownership is what makes losing it hurt. The number on the screen is not information. It is an endowment the system gave you so that it could later threaten to take it away.

Put the two together and the streak is revealed as a machine for _manufacturing a loss you must keep paying to avoid_. Each day you do not act, you do not merely miss a gain; you suffer a loss, at roughly double weight, of an asset the system created and handed to you for free. The activity itself can become irrelevant; you are no longer pursuing a reward, you are fleeing a loss, and fleeing losses is the stronger drive. The trap closes not when the reward gets bigger but when the reference point gets higher, and the reference point is the one thing the designer fully controls.

One more quantitative note, on the business side: loyalty currencies are subject to **breakage**, the industry term for points and rewards that are issued but never redeemed (they expire, or the customer never reaches the threshold). Breakage is a designed-for revenue source: the program books a liability for points outstanding and profits from the fraction that is never claimed. Expiration dates and just-out-of-reach thresholds are tuned to maximize engagement while keeping breakage high, which is to say, tuned so you chase points hard enough to change your behavior but not so easily that you actually collect full value. The points are a leash, and breakage is the part of the leash you paid for and never used.

* * *

### 3. The psychological mechanism

The loyalty program runs on a small, clean set of drives, which is what makes it the clearest specimen in the series.

**Loss aversion** is the core: the streak, tier, or balance becomes an endowment, and the prospect of losing it is felt at roughly double weight, converting a weak "want to continue" into a strong "can't bear to break." **The goal gradient** supplies direction: you are kept perpetually just short of the next stamp, tier, or reward, on the steep part of the motivation curve. **Endowed progress** (the illusion of progress) often seeds the start: "here's 200 welcome points," "you're already Silver," moving your reference point up before you have done anything. And a mild **sunk-cost** effect cements it: the longer the streak or the bigger the balance, the more "wasteful" it feels to abandon, even though the accumulated number is sunk regardless of what you do next.

What is notably _absent_ is the high-variance machinery. There is usually no randomness, no jackpot, no volatility, no near-miss engineered into a reel. The loyalty program does not need them. It captures through the quiet, relentless asymmetry of loss, which is why it feels so different from a slot machine while being, structurally, a member of the same family. It is the family's gentlest cousin, and the most socially acceptable, and for exactly that reason the easiest to underestimate.

* * *

### 4. The business strategy

For a business, loyalty programs do several things at once, and the honest ones and the manipulative ones use the same mechanics for different ends.

**Raise switching costs.** A streak or status tier makes leaving feel like a loss, so customers stay with a worse or pricier option to avoid breaking what they have accumulated. The traveler who books the inferior flight to keep Gold is paying a switching cost the program manufactured. The longer you have been loyal, the more you stand to lose by leaving, which is precisely the lock-in the program is designed to create.

**Increase frequency and spend via the goal gradient.** Keeping customers just short of the next reward or tier pulls extra purchases and visits, especially near thresholds (the well-documented spike in activity as customers approach a reward). The denominator (how many stamps, how many points per tier) is the designer's choice, set to extract the desired behavior.

**Profit from breakage.** Points that expire or are never redeemed are pure margin, so programs are tuned to maximize engagement while keeping a healthy fraction of rewards unclaimed: expiration dates, blackout conditions, and thresholds set just high enough that many never reach them.

**Harvest data and habit.** Loyalty programs are also identity and tracking systems, tying purchases to a person and building the behavioral profile that powers personalization (the recommender feed). The "membership" is, among other things, a consent surface for data collection.

The important fairness point: a loyalty program that rewards behavior the customer genuinely wants (saving money on routine purchases, building a habit they chose) can be a legitimately good deal, a real alignment of interests. The mechanics are neutral; the question is whether the goal the streak serves is _yours_ or only the company's, which is exactly the test from the illusion-of-progress post.

* * *

### 5. The generalization

The loyalty mechanism (loss aversion plus the goal gradient applied to an accumulated, displayed quantity) appears anywhere a system can give you something to lose:

*   **Daily streaks** in language, fitness, meditation, and social apps: the purest modern case, where a flame or a number becomes an endowment you protect, sometimes long after the activity stopped serving you.
*   **Points and stamp cards** in retail, coffee, and groceries: the classic, with breakage and threshold-tuning as the quiet economics.
*   **Airline and hotel status tiers**: loss aversion at its most expensive, where customers reshape real travel decisions to avoid the loss of a status the program invented.
*   **Subscription and membership "benefits"** that accumulate and would be "lost" on cancellation: stored value, accrued perks, and "you'll lose your member pricing" framing that raises the felt cost of leaving.
*   **Gaming login bonuses and daily-reward calendars**: escalating rewards that reset if you miss a day, importing the streak's loss-aversion hook into games (and bridging to the loot-box economy).
*   **Professional and social "reputation" systems**: badges, levels, and karma that, once accumulated, you are reluctant to abandon by leaving the platform.

The unifying structure: **an accumulated, displayed status (streak, tier, balance) that the system endows you with, so that the prospect of losing it (felt at roughly double weight by loss aversion) keeps you engaged, while the goal gradient pulls you toward the next threshold.** No randomness required. The quietest machine in the series, and proof that you do not need a jackpot to capture behavior, only something a person would hate to lose.

* * *

### 6. The defense

The loyalty defense is the friendliest in the series, because many loyalty programs are worth keeping. The goal is not to refuse them but to make sure _you_ own the streak rather than the streak owning you.

**Ask whose goal the counter serves.** A streak or tier is benign exactly when the behavior it tracks is something you independently want (you would exercise, study, or buy these groceries anyway). It has captured you when you are maintaining the number _for its own sake_, doing a joyless token action at 11:50pm or buying things you do not need to reach a threshold. The test is the illusion-of-progress test: is this goal mine, or did the program install it? If the activity stopped serving you but the streak still compels you, the streak is the master.

**Treat accumulated status as sunk, and decide from here.** Loss aversion makes "I'll lose my 100-day streak / my Gold status / my points" feel like a catastrophe, but the accumulated number is already spent value; the only real question is whether the _future_ behavior it demands is worth the _future_ benefit, judged fresh. "I've come so far" and "I don't want to waste it" are precisely the loss-aversion and sunk-cost reflexes the design relies on. Letting a streak break, on purpose, once, is often the cleanest way to discover that the number had more hold on you than the habit did.

**Compute the real value of points and tiers; respect breakage.** Loyalty currency is worth doing arithmetic on: the cash value of points is often small, expiration and thresholds are tuned so much of it is never claimed, and chasing a tier can cost more than the tier is worth. Treat points as a modest discount on things you would buy regardless, never as a reason to spend or to choose a worse option. If keeping status requires reshaping decisions you would otherwise make differently, the program is extracting more than it gives.

**Keep the friendly ones; you do not have to quit everything.** Unlike the casino or the leveraged exchange, a well-aligned loyalty program can be a genuine win. The defense here is discernment, not abstinence: keep the streaks and cards that serve goals you actually hold, and drop the ones that survive only on your reluctance to lose a number.

We have now seen the loudest machines in this series and the quietest one. What is left before the theory is a handful of mechanisms that do not sit anywhere on that loud-to-quiet axis. They work on how the outcome is labeled, on what a gift really costs, on what it costs to walk away, on who you believe you are while you play, on which users the whole apparatus is actually built for, and, at the newest frontier, on a machine that composes the reward itself. The first of them hides in plain sight on every modern slot floor: a machine that throws a party when you lose.

_Next in the series: **The Sound of Losing**, where a payout smaller than your bet is announced as a win._

* * *

## References

*   [Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk](https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185), Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky, Econometrica 47(2): 263-291, 1979
*   [Advances in Prospect Theory: Cumulative Representation of Uncertainty](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00122574), Amos Tversky, Daniel Kahneman, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 5(4): 297-323, 1992
*   [The Loss of Loss Aversion: Will It Loom Larger Than Its Gain?](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcpy.1047), David Gal, Derek D. Rucker, Journal of Consumer Psychology 28(3): 497-516, 2018
*   [The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention](https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkr.43.1.39), Ran Kivetz, Oleg Urminsky, Yuhuang Zheng, Journal of Marketing Research 43(1): 39-58, 2006
*   [Thinking, Fast and Slow](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533557/thinkingfastandslow/), Daniel Kahneman, 2011

I get heated when marketers get paid unfairly.We're often paid less than other roles, despite how much revenue we drive and how much scrutiny our work gets. It's even harder when you don't know what to expect or what to ask for, and most of us don't, especially "in this economy."

I've been on every side of this: I've been paid unfairly myself, set comp for roles as a team lead, helped hundreds of people negotiate their salaries, led marketing at a compensation startup, and even thought about launching my own comp startup pre-MKT1.

It's the newsletter people ask me to update second most often (after [the org chart ones](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/marketing-org-charts)!). 1.   **Most job posts now list salary.** When I wrote the 2022 newsletter, only Colorado's pay transparency law required this. Now [more and more US states](https://www.hrdive.com/news/pay-transparency-law-tracker-states-that-require-employers-to-post-pay-range-or-wage-range/622542/) require companies to list salary, and 87% of the open marketing jobs I checked include a salary. _Now can we require this for equity compensation too?!_

2.   **I can analyze publicly available data at scale.** With Claude Code and the research skills from my [State of Marketing report](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/state-of-marketing-report-part-3-how-to-research-in-claude-code), I can research hundreds of companies and make the graphs in a few workdays. _You can too, and I’m even sharing the [updated research skill](https://mcp.mkt1.co/run/general-research?utm\_source=substack&utm\_medium=email&utm\_campaign=newsletter-2026-10-marketing-salaries-2026) I used in the MKT1 MCP._

3.   **Startup valuations are all over the map, which makes it especially hard to value equity.** AI startups have multi-billion-dollar valuations that seem to go up by the day, while private equity buys SaaS startups for way less than their peak valuations. _Don't worry, I'm not going to write yet another think-piece about Bending Spoons._

4.   **A few companies (OpenAI & Anthropic especially) pay really high salaries for every role.** Should this impact what you ask for at other AI startups?

5.   **Entry-level jobs are scarce, and getting any job is hard.** Should we just take what we can get?

**So I built this analysis based on 1,100+ marketing job posts, 794 from private B2B startups. I hope this serves as a reference when you ask for a raise, get an offer, or make an offer.**Here are the stats that stood out most:

[![Image 1: Six stat cards titled "State of B2B Marketing Salaries: Highlights." They show a $169K median salary for jobs below Director, a $235K median salary for Director and above, $1.17 at recently raised startups and $1.63 at frontier labs for every $1 elsewhere, 12% of roles paying variable comp, and 2 job posts with equity amounts.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6vdJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa2a558c4-7f73-4438-a1e0-516415663fb3_2400x738.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6vdJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa2a558c4-7f73-4438-a1e0-516415663fb3_2400x738.png)

*   **The median salary is $169K for jobs below Director and $235K for Director and above**, so moving into a leadership role is worth about $66K. But only about 1 in 5 job posts is Director or above (169 of 794), so there are far fewer of these jobs to go around (and to analyze).

*   **The fastest path to more salary for the same level, besides getting a job at OpenAI or Anthropic, is to join a startup that raised money in the last year:****They pay about 17% more.**_Note: The green $1 cards show what a job pays for every $1 you’d get at the same level elsewhere._

*   As for the other parts of comp, bonus and equity: **Only 12% of marketing job posts mention a bonus or commission** on top of base, and about 1 in 3 of those hedge it with something like "may be eligible." About 64% of job posts mention equity, but I could only find 2 job posts (not a typo, actually just 1+1) that stated an equity range.

## In this newsletter:

_This is the 1st in a 2-part series, and it has 20+ graphs about the current state of marketing salaries, based on live job posts from Sept 2026._

*   **[Salary data from 1,100+ marketing job posts](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/salary-data-from-1100-marketing-job-posts)** (794 from private B2B startups)

    *   [By level and years of experience](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/salary-data-from-1100-marketing-job-posts)

    *   [By area of marketing](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/marketing-salary-breakdown-by-area-of-marketing), from generalists to ecosystem marketers

    *   [By company](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/marketing-salary-breakdown-by-company-details): Location, OpenAI & Anthropic, AI-native and fundraising

    *   [What's changed since my 2022 report](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/how-salaries-have-changed-since-2022)

*   **[Equity by stage](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/equity-by-stage)** and what you need to evaluate an equity offer

*   **[Methodology](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/more-methodology)**

*   **[Appendix for paid subscribers: More salary graphs:](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/appendix-more-salary-graphs)** Variable comp, company size, stage, funding and category

*   **The skills behind this report:** Search open jobs for free, or access all the data and run the research skills behind this report (paid subscribers only). [Install the MKT1 MCP](https://mcp.mkt1.co/install?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=newsletter-2026-10-marketing-salaries-2026).

*   **Coming next, Part 2: Open Roles Data.**  
When making this salary report, I accidentally (and then on purpose) gathered a bunch of data on the state of open jobs for marketers at B2B startups, so this topic demands a Part 2!

_[Subscribe to get Part 2 in your inbox.](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/subscribe)_ 

This section answers questions like: **What should you get paid at your level and for your years of experience? How much does salary change at each level?**

[![Image 3: Range chart titled "Marketing Salary by Level," showing the 25th to 75th percentile of base salary with the median marked for 5 levels. Medians are $119K for early career (0 to 2 years), $160K for mid (3 to 5 years), $178K for senior (6+ years), $225K for Director / Head of, and $300K for VP / CMO. Based on 794 roles at 347 private B2B startups, Sept 2026.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6mSz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fab4b8fc2-cf44-45ca-ad92-374114fd60d4_2400x1460.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6mSz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fab4b8fc2-cf44-45ca-ad92-374114fd60d4_2400x1460.png)

**The median base salary grows 2.5x+ from early-career roles through marketing leadership roles at the VP and C-level.**

*   **The biggest salary jump happens when you move from Director or Head of to VP or CMO (not a surprise):** VPs & CMOs make a median of $300K vs $225K for Directors / Heads of, a $75K or 33% increase.

    *   The actual increase is likely higher because my sample is mostly VPs, since most CMO roles aren't publicly posted...

_...Or startups just try to get away with not hiring a CMO and keeping marketing a VP-level thing, more on that in [Part 2 of this series](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/subscribe)!_

    *   You don't have to lead all of marketing to get a VP-level salary. VPs of Growth and VPs of Product Marketing make about $69K more than Directors in their area.

    *   If we just look at VPs of Marketing, they make a median of $313K (up from $300K when you combine all types of VPs).

*   **Going from early career to mid-level is a big jump too:** Mid-level marketers make a median of $160K vs $119K at early-career level, a $41K or 34% increase. That means the first few years of your marketing career are when salary grows fastest, until you reach leadership.

_The challenge here is getting an early-career role right now to begin with. That's also a topic for [Part 2 of this series](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/subscribe)._

*   **The smallest jump is from mid to senior level, where all the roles start to blur:** Senior-level marketers make a median of $178K vs $160K at mid-level, only an $18K or 11% increase. Companies don't agree on what "senior" means, so a lot of senior-level jobs are really the same work as mid-level jobs, just asking for a year or 2 more.

*   **Mid-level salaries vary the most of any level below Director:** The middle half of mid-level jobs runs from $135K to $185K, a $50K spread, while senior-level jobs are the tightest, at $165K to $200K. So at mid-level, the company you're talking to matters a lot, and 2 offers for the same years of experience can be very different.

_More on why I organized levels by years of experience until Director level in the [methodology summary below](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/notes-on-methodology)._

*   **The salary ranges overlap:** The top quarter of mid-level jobs make $185K or more, which is more than what the bottom quarter of senior-level jobs make (under $165K). To get paid like you have more years of experience, go to an AI-native, recently funded and/or SF-based company. They pay more at almost every level. _More on this in the [company details section](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/marketing-salary-breakdown-by-company-details) below._

[![Image 4: Range chart titled "Marketing Salary by Years of Experience," showing the 25th to 75th percentile of base salary by the years of experience a job post asks for. Medians are $125K for 0 to 2 years, $160K for 3 to 5, $180K for 6 to 8, $218K for 9 to 10, and $247K for 11+ years.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5Pf8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F823304c6-069c-40f2-90e2-da0f4bc26a85_2400x1502.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5Pf8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F823304c6-069c-40f2-90e2-da0f4bc26a85_2400x1502.png)

**Salary about doubles from 0 to 2 years of experience ($125K) to 11+ years ($247K).**

*   This graph uses only years of experience, with titles stripped out, even for Director and VP roles. The graph stops at 11+ because job posts rarely ask for more than 10 years, even for VP roles (only 26 job posts ask for 11 or more years).

*   **The more experience a job asks for, the more salaries vary.** At 11+ years, salaries range from $185K for a [Head of Marketing at Aboon](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/aboon/8d28b9ed-b14f-48da-ac37-ac64d0c1b599) to $350K for a [VP of Product Marketing at Moloco](https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/moloco/jobs/7981801003). At this point, your title matters more for your salary than your years of experience.

*   **The smallest jump is from 3 to 5 years of experience to 6 to 8 years**, only $20K ($160K to $180K). The biggest comes right after, $38K from 6 to 8 years to 9 to 10 years ($180K to $218K), likely because that's when many jobs become Director or Head of roles.

*   **Early in your career, the title doesn't always match the job.** About 1 in 2 jobs with a junior title (Coordinator, Associate, Specialist or Junior) ask for 3+ years of experience, and the median is 3 years. The title also changes the salary. Among jobs that ask for 0 to 2 years, ones with titles like Marketing Manager make a median of $130K vs $105K for ones titled Associate, Coordinator or Specialist, a $25K or 24% increase (small samples).

[![Image 5: Six stat cards titled "State of B2B Marketing Salaries: Research Overview." They show 1,121 total jobs in the report, 794 B2B startup marketing jobs, 409 total companies, 2,255 job posts reviewed, 1,600+ career pages checked, and 87% of jobs listing a salary.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dDzw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb019a91-f090-4cf5-9e2a-9314b5c8030e_2400x738.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dDzw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb019a91-f090-4cf5-9e2a-9314b5c8030e_2400x738.png)

Before we go further, here's what you need to know to read the graphs:

*   **What's in the data:** 1,121 US, full-time marketing job posts that list a salary. Most of the report uses the 794 at 347 private B2B startups.

*   **Salary:** Most job posts list a salary range, not one number, so I used the midpoint of each range. Example: A job that lists $150K to $190K is $170K in my data. Most graphs show the median of those midpoints, plus the range where the middle half of jobs fall (the 25th to 75th percentile).

*   **Levels:** Below Director, I grouped by years of experience, not by title. 0 to 2 years is early career, 3 to 5 is mid and 6+ is senior level. Director and above, I grouped by title.

*   **What's left out of the main graphs:** Public companies and OpenAI & Anthropic are only in the graphs that compare them to startups.

*   **Small samples:** A blank section in a graph means I couldn't find enough jobs. An asterisk* means a small sample.

*   **Timing:** This is a snapshot of jobs open in September 2026. It shows what companies are offering now, not what people in these roles are earning today.

_I included [more methodology details](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/more-methodology) at the bottom of the newsletter, before [the Appendix](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/appendix-more-salary-graphs) (which has even more graphs for paid subscribers!)._

This section answers questions like: **Which area of marketing pays the most? What does your specific role pay?**

[![Image 6: Table titled "Median Marketing Salary by Role & Level," with a row for each of 9 areas of marketing and columns for early career, mid, senior, Director / Head of, and VP / CMO. The bottom row shows the median of all roles: $119K, $160K, $178K, $225K and $300K. Highlights include product marketing and marketing design at $180K at mid, comms / PR lowest at mid at $129K, and generalists highest at VP / CMO at $313K.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SlEK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feac60efa-bcab-483d-91f9-e7a2044a5f99_2400x1904.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SlEK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feac60efa-bcab-483d-91f9-e7a2044a5f99_2400x1904.png)

**At mid-level, the sub-function you specialize in can mean a $51K difference in salary.**

*   **Product marketing pays the most of all sub-functions.** Product marketers make a median of $180K at mid-level (tied with marketing design) and $194K at senior level (only generalists make more), vs $160K and $178K for all roles. At Director and VP, product marketers make about the same as everyone else. _More in the [product marketing section](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/218278159/whats-the-breakdown-by-level-for-each-marketing-sub-function) below._

*   **Events and field is the only sub-function that pays below the median at every level from mid-level up:** $135K vs $160K at mid-level, $167K vs $178K at senior level, and $208K vs $225K at Director / Head of.

*   **The gap between areas shrinks as you move up.** At mid-level, the gap between the highest- and lowest-paid sub-functions is $51K ($180K for product marketing and design vs $129K for comms and PR). By VP, the variation is only $17K ($313K for VPs of Marketing vs $296K for VPs of Product Marketing). **So your area of marketing matters most in the middle of your career.**

[![Image 7: Range chart titled "Marketing Generalist Salary by Level," showing the 25th to 75th percentile of base salary by level. Medians are $85K early career, $145K mid, $200K senior, $230K Director / Head of, and $313K VP / CMO, with early, senior and VP marked as small samples. Based on 64 roles at 59 startups.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ujLF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff048e0b8-e735-465d-aaee-55543f4fc7c8_2400x1420.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ujLF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff048e0b8-e735-465d-aaee-55543f4fc7c8_2400x1420.png)

**Generalists make the most at senior level and VP / CMO ($200K at senior level and $313K at VP / CMO, the highest of any area) but less than everyone else early on ($85K vs $119K for all roles).**_The fact that junior generalists, especially those that are true [Gen Marketers](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/gen-marketer), make less doesn’t seem fair to me._

*   **The top-paying jobs in the study list salaries up to $400K or more.** They include:

    *   [SVP, Influencer Strategy & Marketing at Salesforce](https://salesforce.wd12.myworkdayjobs.com/External_Career_Site/job/California---San-Francisco/SVP--Influencer-Strategy---Marketing_JR359843) ($373K to $465K, _should I apply?!_)

    *   [CMO at EliseAI](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/EliseAI/750f55ac-8a38-45db-abe8-e6637772256e) ($300K to $450K)

    *   [Head of Brand at Ramp](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/30323399-3039-499d-a0b6-a891ced89e1e) ($309K to $424K)

    *   [Head of Ads Enterprise Marketing at OpenAI](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/openai/a7f4ec2e-e93f-4f81-892a-cd8381f347fe) ($374K to $415K)

    *   [Head of Community, Enterprise Marketing at Anthropic](https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/anthropic/jobs/5388719008) ($400K)

    *   [Head of Marketing at DualEntry](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/dualentry/c41cc85f-9f1f-47e8-8311-8a198212dc9f) ($300K to $400K)

*   **The lowest-paying jobs in the study have salaries as low as $50K**(these aren’t on the graph because they fall below the 25th percentile). They include a Marketing Associate job in SF ($50K to $70K), an Assistant Marketing Manager job in Ohio ($54K to $90K) and a mid-level Product Marketing Manager job at a public company ($62K to $80K).

[![Image 8: Range chart titled "Growth / Demand Gen Salary by Level," showing the 25th to 75th percentile of base salary by level. Medians are $125K early career, $156K mid, $178K senior, $229K Director / Head of, and $298K VP / CMO, with early and VP marked as small samples. Based on 171 roles at 129 startups.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2zB9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F139b8e86-f47b-4d30-ba43-22cad879e9cf_2400x1420.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2zB9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F139b8e86-f47b-4d30-ba43-22cad879e9cf_2400x1420.png)

**Growth salaries fall right at the overall median at every level.** In the past, I often saw growth marketing roles get paid more than other areas of marketing (with the exception of PMM), but that doesn't seem to be the case!

*   **SEO / AEO / web jobs pay the most in growth at some levels, but not all:** They're on top at mid-level ($165K, tied with general growth jobs) and at Director ($254K, a small sample). At senior level, paid jobs pay the most ($193K vs $175K for SEO / AEO / web).

*   **Demand gen jobs pay the least at mid-level:** $138K vs $165K for general growth. That's likely about who's hiring: Demand gen jobs are less often at AI-native startups or startups that have recently raised. By senior level, the gap goes away ($173K vs $165K). _Is this a sign the ti

kept.heading: TIKTOK'S AGENT CHECKOUT ENTERS THE RACE (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: TikTok announced Shopping Assistant and Buy Direct at Advertising Week NYC on October 5, both now in eligibility-based testing in the US. Shopping Assistant is a conversational agent that handles product details, sizing, and availability, then hands the purchase to the in-app browser. Buy Direct is a one-click checkout inside the For You feed using stored payment and address details. Both run on Google's Universal Commerce Protocol, and the brand remains the merchant of record.
kept.article_text:
Title: TikTok’s Agent Checkout Enters the Race — Inside the Feed, Not on the Merchant Site

URL Source: https://forkast.news/tiktoks-agent-checkout-enters-the-race-inside-the-feed-not-on-the-merchant-site/

Published Time: 2026-10-06T09:56:28+00:00

Markdown Content:
Analysis

Shopping Assistant and Buy Direct collapse discovery and transaction into TikTok's algorithmic flow, powered by Google's Universal Commerce Protocol. But the merchant liability question every checkout surface is avoiding remains unanswered.

![Image 1: A pen-and-ink engraving of a marketplace where a merchant stall merges with a customer basket - discovery and transaction collapsing into one flow](https://forkast.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/tiktok-agent-checkout-feed-1024x572.jpg)

On October 5, 2026, at Advertising Week NYC, TikTok announced two features, Shopping Assistant and Buy Direct, that integrate discovery and transaction into a single flow. These tools represent a move toward [agentic commerce](https://forkast.news/glossary/agentic-commerce/), aiming to reduce the friction of leaving the feed to complete a purchase.

## What TikTok launched

Shopping Assistant is a conversational AI agent designed to operate across various TikTok touchpoints. It is built to understand context, retain user preferences, and handle product details, sizing, and availability within a single conversation. If a user decides to purchase, the assistant hands off the transaction to the platform’s in-app browser. Complementing this is Buy Direct, a one-click checkout feature that allows users to complete purchases without ever leaving the For You feed. This system utilizes stored payment methods and saved addresses, with order tracking managed entirely in-app. The features are currently in eligibility-based testing within the U.S. market.

## Structural distinction

The architecture behind these features relies on a familiar set of partners, including Shopify, Salesforce, Shoplazza, and Stripe. The brand remains the merchant of record for every transaction. This structure mirrors the recent launch of [Constructor’s Stripe-powered checkout](https://forkast.news/constructors-stripe-powered-checkout-makes-the-welcome-posture-actionable-and-the-liability-gap-visible/), which also debuted on October 5. These moves reflect a trend where platforms are providing the infrastructure for agent-native checkout, while the underlying mechanics of who is responsible when an agent makes a mistake remain largely unaddressed.

## UCP as convergence

The integration is powered by the [Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)](https://forkast.news/glossary/universal-commerce-protocol-ucp/), an open standard launched by Google in January 2026. UCP serves as a signal of protocol convergence, connecting TikTok to a broader ecosystem that includes major retailers like Walmart, Target, and Best Buy, alongside payment giants like Visa and Mastercard. By adopting this standard, TikTok is positioning itself as a participant in a standardized agent commerce network rather than an isolated walled garden.

## Scale and market impact

According to eMarketer, TikTok Shop generated approximately $15.8 billion in U.S. sales in 2025, a 108% year-over-year increase, with projections reaching $23.4 billion in 2026. With 51% of U.S. social commerce buyers already active on the platform, the potential for agent-native checkout to accelerate these numbers is substantial. A report from PF Global suggests the platform already has a significant economic footprint, with 54 million Americans having purchased items after watching a TikTok video. For marketers, the platform remains a priority; Kantar’s 2026 Media Reactions report ranks TikTok as the number one platform where advertisers plan to increase their spend in 2027.

## The merchant liability gap

Despite the technical progress, the [merchant liability gap](https://forkast.news/the-agentic-commerce-liability-gap-who-pays-when-the-agent-buys-wrong/) persists. PYMNTS Intelligence data from September 2026 indicates that 93% of merchants believe AI providers should bear the financial loss for agent errors. However, there is currently no clean reason code for “agent error” in existing payment infrastructure, nor is there a standardized dispute resolution framework. While Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay provide signaling, they do not re-allocate liability for non-fraudulent errors. Even with American Express launching Agent Purchase Protection in April 2026, the necessary cart context specifications remain under development.

## What TikTok did not say

TikTok has not released public test data regarding the reliability of Shopping Assistant or Buy Direct. The platform’s current communication strategy focuses on the broader potential of AI to transform advertiser content creation rather than the specific operational risks of agent-delegated purchasing. This silence is consistent with the broader industry posture, where the excitement of deployment often outpaces the resolution of structural risks. As retailers navigate the [three distinct postures](https://forkast.news/the-doors-are-locked-how-retailer-postures-are-stalling-the-agent-commerce-stack/)—the QVC welcome, the Kate Spade browse-block, and the Amazon block—TikTok is choosing the former, prioritizing feed convenience over the resolution of liability questions.

## Unresolved liability

The transition to agent-native checkout is moving from theoretical discussion to platform-level implementation. With [Shopify having enabled agent-readiness](https://forkast.news/shopify-embraces-metas-muse-across-all-stores-as-amazon-blocks-it-and-the-merchant-landscape-splits-in-two/) by default in late 2025, the infrastructure is ready for scale. Yet, as only 11% of SMBs are currently considered agent-ready, the gap between the platform’s capabilities and the average merchant’s ability to manage them remains wide. TikTok has provided the technical interface for these transactions, but the financial and operational liability for errors occurring during agent-led purchasing remains unaddressed.

kept.heading: THE EVIDENCE IS CLEAR: AI SEARCH IS COSTING PUBLISHERS (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI search is reducing the traffic publishers receive from traditional search while AI referrals remain too small to make up the difference. One study found AI Overviews reduced outbound organic clicks by 39.8%. Pew found traditional-result clicks fell from 15% to 8% when an AI summary appeared. Meanwhile, ChatGPT generated just 0.02% of publisher referrals compared with 7.3% from Google Search.
kept.article_text:
Title: The evidence is clear: AI search is costing publishers

URL Source: https://digitalcontentnext.org/blog/2026/10/05/the-evidence-is-clear-ai-search-is-costing-publishers/

Published Time: 2026-10-05T11:34:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: -an AI Search bar with the words Ask me anything. No need to click anything else.-](https://digitalcontentnext.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AISearch.png)

For publishers, it has long seemed obvious that when AI answers a user’s question directly, there is less reason to click through to the source. Over the past year, research has repeatedly confirmed it: controlled experiments with search users, analyses of millions of search queries, studies of click-through rates, and traffic data from thousands of publisher sites all point in the same direction.

The methodologies and measurements differ. But the evidence is clear: When AI-generated answers appear in search, fewer people click through to the sources behind those answers. And while referrals from standalone AI platforms are rising, they remain far too small to offset the traffic publishers are losing from traditional search.

That conclusion stands in contrast to claims that AI-powered search can create more opportunities for sites to be discovered and send publishers higher-quality traffic. As [DCN VP of Research Rande Price recently wrote](https://digitalcontentnext.org/blog/2026/09/15/research-casts-doubt-on-ai-search-value-for-sites-and-searchers/), experimental evidence finds little support for those claims.

No single study can capture the full impact of a discovery ecosystem changing this quickly. But with researchers approaching the question using different methodologies, datasets and measures, declining referral traffic can no longer be dismissed as anecdotal, or AI’s role in that decline as speculation.

## AI answers are reducing clicks

Some of the clearest evidence comes from research designed to isolate the effect of AI answers from everything else happening in search.

In a [randomized field experiment](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6513059), Saharsh Agarwal of the Indian School of Business and Ananya Sen of Carnegie Mellon University studied the browsing behavior of more than 1,000 Google users. When an AI Overview appeared, outbound organic clicks fell 39.8% and zero-click searches increased 34.5%.

Research based on observed search behavior reaches much the same conclusion. [Pew Research Center analyzed nearly 69,000 Google searches](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) made by 900 U.S. adults. Users clicked a traditional search result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, compared with 15% when one did not. Links within the AI summaries themselves attracted clicks on just 1% of visits. [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

And the pattern holds at much larger scale. [Ahrefs analyzed 300,000 keywords](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/) and estimated that the presence of an AI Overview reduced click-through to the top-ranking organic result by 58%. The effect extended down the results page, with estimated declines of 51% for the second-ranked result and 46% for the third.

It is important to note that these studies differ: a controlled experiment, observed browsing behavior, and search click-through data. However, it is clear that each reaches the same conclusion: When AI answers appear, publishers get fewer clicks.

## AI referral traffic is growing, but its not nearly enough

The traffic flowing from AI platforms is growing quickly. It is also nowhere close to replacing the search traffic publishers are losing.

[Reuters Institute’s _Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026_](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026) puts the gap in stark terms. Drawing on Chartbeat data from 2,576 publisher sites, the report found that Google Search referrals fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, including a 38% decline in the U.S. However, the researchers caution that AI Overviews cannot account for all of that decline; algorithm changes, publisher strategies and shifts in audience behavior also play a role.

But the scale of AI referrals offers little evidence of a replacement channel. In the same dataset, Google Search accounted for 7.3% of publisher referrals and Google Discover another 13%. ChatGPT accounted for just 0.02% and Perplexity 0.002%. Google Search alone delivered roughly 500 times as much referral traffic as ChatGPT.

[Sensor Tower’s _State of Web 2026_](https://sensortower.com/report/state-of-web-2026) shows how misleading the growth rates can be. Traffic from AI assistants grew 86% year over year in 2025, while generative AI referrals still accounted for only about 0.7% of overall web traffic.

[Similarweb’s research on AI search](https://aisearch.similarweb.com/blog/ai-search-trends/) finds the same disconnect from another angle: use of AI platforms continued to climb while outbound referral traffic plateaued. More people using AI does not necessarily translate into more traffic for the sites supplying the information.

## Fewer opportunities to monetize and build relationships

The impact of fewer referrals extends well beyond the lost pageview. Every visit gives a publisher the opportunity to serve advertising, convert a subscriber, register a user, promote a newsletter or app, collect first-party data, and build a direct relationship with that person.

AI search changes that exchange. Publisher content can still contribute to satisfying a user’s query, but the visit that historically followed discovery may never happen. The platform retains the user while the publisher loses the opportunity to monetize the interaction or deepen the audience relationship.

That distinction matters because traffic is not simply a distribution metric. For publishers, it is one of the mechanisms through which investment in original content produces economic value. When AI systems satisfy more demand without sending users to the

## AI search is breaking the publisher-platform value exchange

The research now spans controlled experiments, observed user behavior, analyses of hundreds of thousands of keywords, and traffic data from thousands of publisher sites. The measurements vary, but the finding does not: AI-generated answers reduce clicks to publishers, while traffic from AI platforms remains far too small to replace what is being lost.

This changes more than the mechanics of search. For decades, search created an exchange: publishers made their content discoverable, platforms helped users find it, and publishers received traffic in return. AI search is breaking that exchange.

AI systems can increasingly use publisher content to answer a user’s question without delivering that user to the publisher. The content still creates value. What is disappearing is the mechanism that returned some of that value to the companies that invested in creating it.

kept.heading: WHEN TO DO SALES REMOTELY VS IN-PERSON (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The best mix of remote and in-person sales meetings depends on product complexity. Using the right mix can improve sales performance by up to 27.3%. For simple products, about 37.9% of meetings held in person produced the best results, while complex products performed worse when sales teams relied only on remote meetings. In-person meetings help build trust and uncover customer needs, which matters more when products require more customization or evaluation. Sales teams should use more in-person meetings early in complex sales relationships, then reduce them as they learn the customer's needs, while still accommodating customers who prefer remote meetings.

Title: When to do sales remotely vs in-person

URL Source: https://app.sciencesays.com/p/when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person

Published Time: 2026-10-06T10:22:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
**This insight is brought to you by…**[**Modash**](https://mdsh.io/vovmm2rw61?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person)

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e47a5f30-273d-4682-a06a-0032e7f119a5/image.png?t=1790845870)](https://mdsh.io/vovmm2rw61?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person)

Everyone talks about how much the creator economy is worth. But **what does a good influencer marketing salary****look like** these days? That’s data that’s rarely been transparent.

Modash [surveyed 500 influencer marketers](https://mdsh.io/vovmm2rw61?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person) to map real salaries across geography, experience, niche, and workload, including how overtime and job conditions affect pay.

💡 The biggest finding? The job is wildly misunderstood, and influencer marketers feel globally underpaid.

**Topic**: Sales | Customer Experience  
**For**: B2B  
**Research date**: June 2026  
**Universities**: Ruhr University Bochum

#### 📈**Recommendation**

If you’re selling a simple product (e.g. standardized steel pipes) focus more on remote selling.

If your product is complex (e.g. highly customized ERP software), include more in-person interactions with customers. You can then gradually decrease the share of in-person meetings as the sales rep gets to know the customer better.

Your sales team will perform better, leading to more sales.

If a customer prefers to meet remotely, accommodate that regardless of how complex your product is.

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e271e6b0-240c-4e4f-9213-021b02220d33/Insight__343.png?t=1790845373)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   As part of an analysis of 15,172 sales interactions with 3,565 sanitary product customers (e.g. plumbers, architects, contractors), researchers found that:

    *   For simple products (e.g. standardized pipes), holding about 1 in 3 meetings in-person (37.9%) boosted sales performance by 27.3% (vs only in-person meetings)

    *   For complex products (e.g. custom-sized vanity), customers prefer in-person meetings. Doing only remote meetings reduced sales performance by up to 32.4%

    *   For medium complexity products, the optimal number of in-person meetings was 64.1%

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   Remote calls are more efficient but make it [harder to build trust and share concerns](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-020-00750-2?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person). When we meet someone in person, it helps [build a relationship](https://doi.org/10.1509/jmr.15.0243?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person) and understand needs.

*   When we buy [a more complex product](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-021-00803-0?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person), we need to trust the seller, understand their value, and feel they’re meeting our needs. This is done better in-person.

*   When we find in-person meetings too resource-intensive or inefficient, we [appreciate it if a seller](https://doi.org/10.1509/jm.75.2.55?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person) adapts to our needs to meet remotely.

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   This research focused only on relationships with existing customers. It may change for new customers where there is no prior relationship or trust.

*   Different types of meetings are likely better for different stages of the sales cycle (e.g. exploration, proposals, negotiation, renewals).

*   The study looked at a single manufacturer of a wide array of sanitary products for construction. It likely varies by industry (e.g. tech companies may prefer remote meetings while the construction industry may value in-person interactions more).

#### 👀**Real-life example**

RemKliq offers a standardized, plug-and-play product to automate payment follow-ups for companies.

❌**Issue:**Despite being a straightforward product without significant customization, their demos include an option for an in-person walkthrough at the office of potential customers.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2871f9ac-4113-4bb6-a58f-faae5c70d901/343_Example.png?t=1790845558)

✅**Solution:**

*   RemKliq should focus on, and push for, online meetings to increase the efficiency of their sales team.

*   To accommodate customers that really want in-person meetings, they can include a small line underneath the online demo option (e.g. “Click here if you’d prefer to meet us in-person instead.”)

*   This is a good page to include their number of sales, or pageviews, to [provide a social proof](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/case-study-how-to-write-social-proof-numbers) of their effectiveness (e.g. “Automating payment follow-ups for over XX companies”).

*   On their [video calls](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/case-study-closing-more-sales-in-videocalls) with prospective customers, their team should use an unblurred background that shows off the salesperson’s personality and carefully observe and copy the body language of the person they’re speaking to (e.g. lean forward when they do).

#### 📖**Research**

_Remember: This is_ _a new_ _scientific discovery. In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person)_). It may also not be generalizable to your situation. If it’s a risky change, always test it on a small scale before rolling it out widely._

#### 🎁**Bonus: Trivia**

Here is how else Science Says can help you:

*   📈**Join the**[Science Says Platform](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person)to unlock all 300+ insights and exclusive playbooks

*   📘**Boost your results** with [Science-based Playbooks](https://products.sciencesays.com/?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person) (for Pricing, Ad Creatives, Ecommerce, or SaaS)

*   🔬**Get science-based content for your brand**. Publish [groundbreaking insights](https://www.sciencesays.com/enterprise-services?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-to-do-sales-remotely-vs-in-person) about AI, marketing, or management that your customers will love.

🎓 It took our team of PhDs and me **14 hours** to accurately turn this research into this 3-min insight.
