Title: How to survive a double life as an operator-creator

URL Source: https://www.elenaverna.com/p/how-to-survive-a-double-life-as-an

Published Time: 2026-10-05T19:44:22+00:00

Markdown Content:
The best business content creators still have day jobs. Everyone’s got an opinion, but having hands-on experience is what keeps you grounded in reality.

That’s why I’m a big fan of operator-creators.

That’s definitely been my approach. (You can read the full story here if you want: [So you want to be a content creator?](https://www.elenaverna.com/p/so-you-want-to-be-a-content-creator)) Even though my content and advising work is self-sustaining, I keep taking full-time jobs. That’s one of the reasons I’m guessing lovely people like you keep giving me your precious attention by reading stuff I write: because it’s based on what I’ve actually done.

So I’ve got no plans to give either of these sides of my life up. For the most part, they actually make each other better: my day job makes my content much more interesting and relevant and credible. Writing things out forces me to take the stuff floating around in my brain and turn it into frameworks that I can share with other people. And having my own audience is an immediate win for any company where I work - I can help them with product awareness, brand building, talent recruitment, all of that. I’m like a one-woman distribution channel.

But holy gray area.

I’m not trying to hide anything, but it still feels like a double life. You’ve got two identities and sets of obligations to manage at the same time.

So I’ve created some rules for myself to keep me sane.

You don’t want generic ads, right? To make things more valuable for you, I’m featuring stuff I personally recommend - including two webinars this week!

![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cHsj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0fe712ab-22a0-4083-b1d5-ea606afcb8b4_1846x336.png)

**[→ ‘Ask the Experts: Pricing AI products for revenue growth’ with Stripe - this Tuesday, Oct 6th](https://go.stripe.global/ask-the-experts-pricing-ai-products-emea?utm_source=Elena%20Growth%20Scoop&utm_medium=ThirdPartyBuy&utm_campaign=EMEA_Sold_Startups_Pan-EMEA_EN_SLP_PROSP_NativeDemo_Field-SponsoredPost1&utm_content=ask-the-experts-Event-N/A&utm_placement=SLP)**: For any AI or SaaS leaders out there working on your AI pricing (all of us right?), this virtual event looks cool: Sam Lee (Stripe’s head of global pricing) and Andrew Garvin (COO/cofounder at Metronome) are doing a full Q&A on Oct 6. I want to hear how they discuss usage-based vs. hybrid vs. outcome-based.  
**📅 Check it out:[Register for free](https://go.stripe.global/ask-the-experts-pricing-ai-products-emea?utm_source=Elena%20Growth%20Scoop&utm_medium=ThirdPartyBuy&utm_campaign=EMEA_Sold_Startups_Pan-EMEA_EN_SLP_PROSP_NativeDemo_Field-SponsoredPost1&utm_content=ask-the-experts-Event-N/A&utm_placement=SLP).**

**[→ Optimizely’s free Personalization Webinar - this Wednesday, Oct 7th](https://www.optimizely.com/field-notes/events/ai-personalization-webinar-corinthia-hotels/?utm_source=elenaverna&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=global_pers_elenaverna-newsletter-3_q326_tofu_pt_traffic&utm_content=pers-corinthia-hotels-webinar-oct7):** I’m sharing this one because every marketing team says they want personalization at scale… and almost none actually pull it off. This webinar is about a team (Corinthia Hotels) that pulled it off. And everyone’s saying they can 10x productivity with agents, so I love seeing a team that has the receipts. Come see how they did it.  
**📅 Check it out:**[](https://www.optimizely.com/field-notes/events/ai-personalization-webinar-corinthia-hotels/?utm_source=elenaverna&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=global_pers_elenaverna-newsletter-3_q326_tofu_pt_traffic&utm_content=pers-corinthia-hotels-webinar-oct7)**[Register here.](https://www.optimizely.com/field-notes/events/ai-personalization-webinar-corinthia-hotels/?utm_source=elenaverna&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=global_pers_elenaverna-newsletter-3_q326_tofu_pt_traffic&utm_content=pers-corinthia-hotels-webinar-oct7)** It’s free!

**[→ Research Flow by Typeform](https://tfsales.typeform.com/to/q03Il6X2?utm_source=Elena%20Verna&source=Website&source2=Influencer)**: One of the best parts of my [‘What people really think of IC roles’](https://www.elenaverna.com/p/report-what-people-really-think-about) report was getting to hear people share allll the details of how their career has developed. And I was only able to do that because Typeform’s Research Flow lets participants respond out loud and then does live, AI-powered follow-up questions based on those responses. So cool. You should definitely check it out.  
🎁 **Offer: [Schedule a demo and get $500 off](https://tfsales.typeform.com/to/q03Il6X2?utm_source=Elena%20Verna&source=Website&source2=Influencer).**_See terms and conditions._[1](https://www.elenaverna.com/p/how-to-survive-a-double-life-as-an#footnote-1)

This whole scenario can be very blurry, so my goal is to always be super clear about my commitments and incentives and priorities. I don’t want anyone to be surprised.

This conversation is ideally happening before the first day of work.

It’s not as much of an issue for me these days, because the companies I work with see my content creation as part of why they’re hiring me. Now, they’re not trying to stop me from posting - if anything, they want me to post more. But it was such a key part of my early operator-creator juggling act that I still consider it my #1 rule - make sure they know what you’re doing, and what is and isn’t theirs. This direct conversation is also a good time to set boundaries on what they feel comfortable with me sharing or not sharing in my writing.

If you’ve already got something going, do nottttt try to hide it. If you’ve got a newsletter or a booming LinkedIn profile or YouTube channel or whatever, don’t just treat them like some awkward hobby that you hope nobody notices.

And if you’re just getting started, it’s a good idea to be up front about that too: Tell your manager and/or mentors. Spoiler alert: They’ll probably be excited. Every company is trying to figure out employee-generated content and build-in-public, so if you’re wanting to get your voice out there, they’ll probably be fine with it. They might even help you.

Also: Make sure you read your employee agreement. Make sure you know what you’re literally signing up for when it comes to outside work, IP, conflicts of interest, and confidentiality. Since my content existed before any work agreements I’m signing now, I always make sure that it’s extremely clear that all existing partnerships, content, and audiences stay mine AND I’m explicitly allowed to run my side gigs.

Oh, hey, that’s you. Just like I want to lay it all out there with my employer, I’ve gotta be completely transparent with you - especially you beautiful paid subscribers, since you’re also kind of employing me, too?

Particularly with the general Internet public, trust is everything. I want every single person who sees my stuff to know 100% what my incentives are and where I’m coming from.

In an ideal world, people would see my content gradually over time and recognize the context. But… yeah, no such luck. People see one post and make assumptions. Even doing the ‘These opinions are mine and not my employer’s’ type language gets ignored. So I just try to go out of my way to mention what my connections and context are.

Yep, the other _other_ boss.

Whenever I’m collabing with another company that is not Lovable, it’s particularly important to me that they know which ‘Elena’ they’re getting. Sometimes I’m speaking at conferences as ‘Elena from Lovable.’ But if someone is trying to sponsor this newsletter, they have to know that this doesn’t give them Lovable privileges or access or anything else - that’s just ‘Elena the very public PLG enthusiast.’

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-9S_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9383c2c-0e73-4cfe-8f7e-255c45f7abd2_800x450.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-9S_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9383c2c-0e73-4cfe-8f7e-255c45f7abd2_800x450.png)

So, keeping the right people in the loop is half of it, but the other half is figuring out which boundaries need to be drawn.

We’ll start with the easy one - whose audience is this? Mine! All mine. No touchie!

I’ve spent hundreds? Thousands? Of hours of my life creating this content and building relationships with you nice people, and getting to maintain my own audience across all these companies is something any employer is gonna have to try to pry from my Orangetheory-enhanced grip.

This can get bad without any bad intent at all - both my full-time role and my creator biz take time, and can grow faster if I put more time/thought/energy into them. There’s always some block on my schedule that could go toward the company paying me a salary or toward the business that I personally own.

So this is another one that is easier because I’ve set expectations for myself and been clear with the Lovable team. It’s actually different at different roles I’ve had, but my policy right now is Lovable work has to come first. Fortunately, I don’t have to fight too hard to carve out time for my writing and online conversations, because my posts often lead to more traffic and attention for the brand. So I know that it’s helping the company, too. But if I’m up against a deadline or need to travel, then my content will get pushed back.

This one is very clear to me, but I wish it were more clear to everyone else: My opinion is (almost always) just my opinion.

I didn’t fully appreciate this until Lovable, but now I can’t get away from it. Before, when I wrote about hiring or pricing or management or what I thought of AI, people realized it was just me sharing my perspective. Now, because of my very visible work at Lovable, people are sometimes interpreting stuff I post as an official statement from the company. Even if I never mention the company, or I’m writing about something completely unrelated to my job. Even if I directly say I’m just speaking for myself!

I hate this. I don’t want to stop thinking out loud. Stuff happens so fast now, and I think it’s valuable for me to be able to share my reactions and observations, without putting on the CorpoBot filter.

[![Image 3: shape](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lkj-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6579e4ac-f588-43d6-9909-29fff6d86358_1470x1470.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lkj-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6579e4ac-f588-43d6-9909-29fff6d86358_1470x1470.jpeg)

That’s how I feel about people I follow - I want to hear their for-real, unfiltered takes. I wanna know what they actually think, including the opinions that are half-baked, highly debatable, and even sometimes laughably wrong.

But I also totally get why people make this connection. I’m proud to be associated with Lovable, so it’s not really fair for me to get mad if people… associate me with Lovable. My behavior does reflect on Lovable to some degree. And people may assume that my opinions are part of the company marketing machine, or that I’m just saying something because I was told to, even when I’m totally not. I can’t control every interpretation of what I say.

I haven’t figured this one out. But the rule I’m trying to follow is just: Always try to be clear when I’m speaking for Lovable. And if something is Lovable-adjacent, but I’m NOT speaking for Lovable, I also try to be very clear about that, too. But outside of that, please just assume that stuff I say/write is you getting a look straight to the inside of my thoughts-still-in-progress brain.

Oof, this one gets tricky. The fact that I’m in the weeds with a company gives me all the context that makes my perspective credible and interesting. But being in The Room Where It Happens gives me access to tons of info that is not public knowledge.

So what are the boundaries between my honest takes based on my internal experience, vs. revealing insider information that could hurt the company? Yeah. Tricky. Internal numbers, our specific strategies, failed experiments, private decisions, etc etc etc. I’m sure lots of people (especially our competitors, lol) would love to hear all about that stuff. And it is _very_ interesting. But I need to maintain boundaries around what is okay to share with the outside world.

Fortunately, Lovable’s very committed to the whole [Build In Public strategy](https://www.elenaverna.com/p/building-in-public-is-scary-do-it). We share a lot on purpose, and there’s an awesome culture of being open and honest, even about the hard stuff. But that doesn’t mean that company secrets or every internal conversation is up for grabs.

This one has got to be the messiest. A ‘brand’ is all about associations and mental connections and how people see you. This is where it’s nice having things all lined up, where my personal content supports my full-time work and makes everyone’s brand better.

But I still try to be super careful when it comes to situations where it seems like my personal brand is benefiting from the Lovable brand.

Like, when a company wants to sponsor me, or an event wants me to be a speaker. Are they asking about this because of my content and my personal brand? Or is this because of my role at Lovable?

And that’s where the expectation setting comes in. Especially when money is changing hands, I’m always ultra clear when I’m operating as “Elena the Content Creator” and “Elena from Lovable.”

And I’m also careful about how a connection might reflect back on Lovable - because ‘they’re not a direct Lovable competitor’ isn’t enough anymore. These days, direct competition is just scratching the surface of potential conflicts of interest - lots of other orgs are potential partners, vendors, customers, or acquisition targets. Which means my interactions with them could reflect on Lovable. And with how fast AI products change, any company that is firmly in one of those buckets is just as likely to launch a directly competitive product in the next day or two.

It can be so hard to tell. So I’m always a bit cautious. To the point where even if everything lines up on paper, I may not do it.

I tried to map these out as rules, but the lines can be so wavy. So, I just say: when in doubt, bail out.

There have been opportunities that were probably fine, not competitive, fully disclosed, and crazy good money that I still didn’t end up doing. Something about them just felt off. Usually because I could imagine someone seeing the post or whatever and misunderstanding my incentives or motivations. Or because I noticed myself doing serious mental gymnastics to explain to myself why it was technically okay.

I’ve learned not to spend too much time talking myself out of that feeling. The trust I’ve built with you, with my employer, with sponsors is all stuff I can’t get back. It’s not worth putting that at risk.

Like, for me, one of the big ones is sponsored social content - it’s definitely not _wrong_, but it feels… muddy. Since my social presence is much more tied to my day-to-day ops stuff, dropping a paid endorsement for another company into the stream feels a bit off for me, even if it’s totally disclosed.

So I’ve handled that by separating surfaces - I don’t do #ads on LinkedIn, but this newsletter works more like a standard media property, where sponsors are a normal part of the biz. But even then, I’m pretty selective about who I let sponsor these posts - in general, it’s only products I use or am at least exploring, so that I feel good recommending that you spend your time checking them out.

That’s kind of my point through all of this: Being an operator-creator is an amazing flywheel. Solving hard problems for cool companies means great stories and insights that turn into interesting content. Interesting content attracts large groups of interesting people. And having access to all of these interesting people helps to connect me to more great companies and their lovely challenges. It builds over time and can for sure be a win for everyone.

Just as long as you don’t get too greedy. Don’t try to cheat on either side. Don’t share info that your company would be mad about. Don’t spam your loyal audience with feature launch announcements that aren’t relevant to them, or the product ads that you’d never use yourself. Just pay attention to the tricky overlap spots and be honest with your boss(es) and you’ll have a much better shot at keeping control of your multiple personalities.

_Edited by [Jonathan Yagel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jwbyagel/)._

kept.article_text:
Title: 10 Halloween emails from last year to inspire your campaigns - Email Love

URL Source: https://emaillove.com/halloween-email-examples-to-inspire-your-campaigns

Published Time: 2026-10-01T10:35:27-07:00

Markdown Content:
It’s October, so Halloween isn’t far off, and the first Halloween emails are already showing up in our inboxes. [Michaels](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-michaels-230), [See’s Candies](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-sees-candies-477), and [Sharper Image](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-sharper-image-754) all sent theirs in the last week of September. If you’re still working out what to send this year, it helps to see what other brands did last time, so we went back through the Halloween emails we saved last October and picked ten of our favorites to inspire your campaigns.

A lot of Halloween emails look the same, with an orange and black palette, a pumpkin in the hero, and a sale with “spooktacular” somewhere in the subject line. The ones below stood out because the brand tied Halloween back to what their product actually does, or because they tried something with the content we hadn’t seen before. They were sent anywhere from October 6 to Halloween itself, so there’s still time to plan something similar. Each one includes the subject line and send date, and you can click through to see the full email on Email Love.

* * *

## 1. Zound turned hearing damage into a horror movie

![Image 1: Zound Halloween email: The Ringing horror movie poster](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/zound-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Watch this Halloween Horror 🫣 · Sent October 29, 2025

Zound sells earplugs for concerts and festivals, which isn’t an obvious fit for Halloween. They got around that by making the whole hero a poster for a horror film called The Ringing. The tagline is “They went to the concert without protection,” it’s starring “You (without your earplugs),” and there’s a fake rating box that says it’s restricted for relentless ringing and permanent regret.

What we like is that the joke and the product pitch are the same thing. You can’t get the poster without also getting why you’d want earplugs. The rest of the email is short: a line asking if you want to star in a movie with a better ending, a 2×2 grid of the four colorways, and one Shop Now button.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-zound-103)

* * *

## 2. Ketone-IQ backed up its zombie joke with some scary stats

![Image 2: Ketone-IQ Halloween email: Fuel for the Living](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/ketone-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** 🪦 Don’t be a Zombie… · Sent October 31, 2025

Ketone-IQ sent this one on Halloween. The hero says “Fuel for the Living” over a row of grey zombie hands reaching up, with one human hand in the middle holding a bottle of Ketone-IQ. The copy carries the idea on: most people are “wandering through life like energy-deprived zombies.”

The next section is what makes it work. Three big stat boxes say 88% of Americans are metabolically unhealthy, 75% are overweight or obese, and 34% are pre-diabetic, followed by “But you don’t have to join the energy undead.” The button says Escape the Energy Graveyard. It’s a good example of a health brand using a Halloween joke to make a serious point without it feeling heavy.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-ketone-iq-team-41)

* * *

## 3. Rest wants your old sheets to become ghost costumes

![Image 3: Rest Halloween email: Put Your Old Bedding to Rest](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/rest-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** 🛏️ Spooky Sale Starts Now · Sent October 16, 2025

Rest makes cooling bedding, and its Halloween email is built around a pun on the brand name: “Put your old bedding to rest.” The hero photo is a group of people dressed as ghosts in old bedsheets, with the line “You’ve held onto your old sheets long enough. Maybe it’s time they serve a new purpose this Halloween.”

The sale itself is up to 35% off, but the story gives you a reason to replace your sheets that has nothing to do with the discount. It also stays on brand with a dark blue palette instead of orange and black, and the product copy keeps the theme going with “no jump scares from night sweats.”

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-rest-72)

* * *

## 4. Brightland told some olive oil horror stories

![Image 4: Brightland Halloween email: Olive Oil Horror Stories](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/brightland-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Olive Oil Horror Stories 👻 · Sent October 15, 2025

Brightland’s email is really a competitive comparison dressed up for Halloween. Under a dark, candlelit hero that says “Olive Oil Horror Stories,” it walks through three numbered problems with supermarket olive oil: oils labeled just “olive oil” or “light,” vague “Product of Italy/Spain/Greece” labels that hide blends, and clear bottles that go rancid under store lights. Each one is followed by how Brightland handles it.

The call to action is Read the Blog, not Shop Now. It’s a good model if your brand doesn’t have a natural Halloween angle, because the theme is just the wrapper for something that teaches the reader something.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-b-r-i-g-h-t-l-a-n-d-45)

* * *

## 5. Uber found a ride for every mummy and monster

![Image 5: Uber Halloween email: No Tricks. Just Trips.](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/uber-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Take 40% off rides spooky season 👻 · Sent October 27, 2025

Uber’s email opens with “No tricks. Just trips.” over a white car and some bats on a black and purple background. The offer is 40% off your first trip, up to $10. The part we keep coming back to is the module below it, where Uber lists its ride types and rewrites each description for Halloween. UberXL has “space for every mummy, monster, and mate,” Uber Black is for “a hauntingly stylish entrance,” and Wait & Save lets you “scare up savings.”

None of that needed a new template. It’s Uber’s standard product module with new copy, and it reminds you that Halloween night is a night when a lot of people need a ride home from a party.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-uber-16)

* * *

## 6. TUSHY went for the bathroom humor

![Image 6: TUSHY Halloween email: It's always spooky season if you wipe](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/tushy-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Is your butt going as a skidmark for Halloween? · Sent October 6, 2025

TUSHY was one of the earliest Halloween sends we saved last year, and it’s one of the funniest. The hero says “It’s always spooky season if you wipe” over a pyramid of toilet paper rolls with a few bats flying around it, on a soft peach background. The first button says “Cleanse yourself,” and the body copy is about reversing “the curse of wiping.”

The email is short and sells one product. It shows how a brand with a strong voice can use a holiday to make the same point it always makes. The press logos at the bottom (VICE, CNN Underscored, The New Yorker, goop) help with a product some people are still unsure about.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-morgan-from-tushy-86)

* * *

## 7. Pamos mixed a Halloween cocktail with skull ice cubes

![Image 7: Pamos Halloween email: Buzzed to the Bone cocktail](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/pamos-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Try This Spirit-Lifting Cocktail 👻 · Sent October 13, 2025

Halloween drink recipes were everywhere last October. De Soi, Cumulus Coffee, Soul, and Harmless Harvest all sent one. The Pamos version stood out for its art direction. “Buzzed to the Bone” is set in a vintage orange serif over a photo of a skeleton, a bottle, and two red cocktails with skull-shaped ice cubes, with the line “High spirits, zero horrors.”

The recipe itself is easy to follow, with measurements for each ingredient and a one-line method, and the button says Mix the Magic. After that, the email moves on to the rest of the product range and a store locator, so it still works as a sales email.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-pamos-14)

* * *

## 8. Škoda UK turned a car boot into a monster and asked readers to make their own

![Image 8: Skoda UK DRIVEN newsletter: The Spooky Edit](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/skoda-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Something frighteningly fun for Hallowe’en, Andy. · Sent October 22, 2025

Car brand newsletters are usually model news and finance offers, so this one surprised us. Škoda UK’s DRIVEN newsletter opens with “The Spooky Edit” and a photo of a Škoda with its boot turned into a monster, complete with eyes, paper teeth, and a big red tongue. The intro is written by Hattie Newman, a papercraft maker and director, who made the “Šcary Škoda” and walks you through how she did it in a how-to video.

Then it asks readers to make their own “boot beast” and send in a photo for a chance to win one of three £500 shopping vouchers. Further down, it announces the winner of the previous competition, a reader named Kirsty whose photo of her Kodiaq at a campsite won her a camping kit. That’s a newsletter that creates its own content for the next issue, and it gives people something to actually do on Halloween instead of something to buy. The model news and EV updates are still in there, they just aren’t the lead.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-skoda-uk-2)

* * *

## 9. Tushbaby’s customers made their babies part of the costume

![Image 9: Tushbaby Halloween email: Happy Halloween customer photos](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/tushbaby-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** Meet the ultimate Halloween Hack 🎃 · Sent October 31, 2025

Tushbaby sent this one on Halloween itself, and it opens with a grid of four photos of parents in costume carrying their kids in costume: a beekeeper with a baby bee, a Top Gun family, and Princess Leia carrying a little Grogu. They look like they came from customers rather than a studio shoot, and the line under the headline calls them “parent favorites.”

The subject line frames the hip carrier as a trick-or-treating hack, and the rest of the email backs that up with a cowgirl mom carrying a baby dressed as a cow, then copy about saving your back and keeping your hands free on the night. It finishes with a multi-brand family sweepstakes and an SMS sign-up for early Black Friday access. Photos of the product being used on the night are more convincing than a studio shot, and it’s a good reminder to ask your customers for their Halloween photos.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-tushbaby-37)

* * *

![Image 10: Goldbelly Halloween email: Last Chance for Halloween](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/10/goldbelly-halloween-2025.jpg)

**Subject line:** LAST CHANCE for Halloween! 🎃💀 · Sent October 27, 2025

A lot of last-chance emails are a countdown and a button. Goldbelly’s opens with “Last chance for Halloween” and a mummy cake, tells you that you have to order today for Halloween delivery, and then shows a full grid of Halloween desserts. Each tile names the bakery and the city it ships from, like Edgar’s Bakery in Birmingham and Flour Shop in Los Angeles, so you can see where each dessert comes from.

The email uses bright orange, purple, and yellow blocks of color, and each product sits in its own tile. Below the grid, Goldbelly is already promoting the PieCaken for Thanksgiving and a Double Points October offer, so the email still has something to sell after October 31.

[See the full email](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-goldbelly-26)

* * *

## A few more we almost picked

There were a few others we liked. [Lactaid](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-lactaid-2) sent Halloween recipes made by Instagram creators and credited each one by handle. [De Soi](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-de-soi-98) sent a Witches’ Brew recipe with edible purple glitter. [Cumulus Coffee](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-cumulus-coffee-42) turned an espresso martini into “an elixir only a spell could summon.” [Harmless Harvest](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-harmless-harvest-61) dressed its coconut water bottles up as a vampire and a fairy. And [Marley Spoon](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-marley-spoon-6) skipped orange and black altogether for mint and aqua.

* * *

## What the best Halloween emails had in common

Looking at all of these together, a few things show up again and again.

*   **The theme connects to the product.**[Zound](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-zound-103), [Ketone-IQ](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-ketone-iq-team-41), [Rest](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-rest-72), [Brightland](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-b-r-i-g-h-t-l-a-n-d-45), and [TUSHY](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-morgan-from-tushy-86) each found a Halloween idea that only works for what they sell. If you swapped in another brand’s logo, the email wouldn’t make sense.
*   **Customer and creator content stands out.**[Škoda UK](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-skoda-uk-2) handed its newsletter to a papercraft artist and asked readers to send in their own creations, and [Tushbaby](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-tushbaby-37) led with families wearing its carriers on the night.
*   **You don’t need orange and black.**[Rest](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-rest-72) stayed in dark blue, [Škoda UK](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-skoda-uk-2) in green, [Tushbaby](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-tushbaby-37) in soft beige, and [Marley Spoon](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-marley-spoon-6) in mint and aqua, and they all still read as Halloween emails.
*   **New copy can be enough.**[Uber](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-uber-16) kept its usual product module and rewrote the descriptions. If your team doesn’t have time to design a seasonal template, start there.
*   **The subject lines are funny.**[“Olive Oil Horror Stories”](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-b-r-i-g-h-t-l-a-n-d-45) and [“Is your butt going as a skidmark for Halloween?”](https://emaillove.com/email-inspiration-from-morgan-from-tushy-86) both give people a reason to open before they’ve seen the design.

* * *

## See more Halloween emails

There are plenty more Halloween emails in the [Email Love Halloween collection](https://emaillove.com/inspiration/halloween), including this year’s sends as they come in. If you’re planning your own campaign, it’s worth a scroll to see what your competitors did last October.

And if your team designs emails in Figma, the [Email Love Figma plugin](https://emaillove.com/) lets you build a seasonal email like any of these and export it as production-ready code for your ESP, so you can spend your time on the idea instead of the rebuild.

kept.heading: I EDIT 115+ ARTICLES PER YEAR. HERE ARE THE 5 WAYS I EDIT DRAFTS (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Semrush's senior blog editor shares her editing best practices, from fact-checking to giving more feedback than you think you should.

Title: I edit 115+ articles per year. Here are the 5 ways I edit drafts.

URL Source: https://www.semrush.com/blog/my-editing-approaches-framework/

Published Time: 2026-09-17T13:34:00Z

Markdown Content:
Semrush publishes hundreds of blog articles every year. Each one needs editorial review, and most need revisions before they’re ready for publication. As a Senior Editor, I make that process happen.

What the editing for a given article actually entails is pretty varied. We cover a lot of topics, work with many writers, and balance competing priorities.

So, I simply can’t treat every piece the same way. But I also can’t invent a completely new approach whenever it’s time for me to edit content. (I did that initially, and it didn’t go well.)

Instead, I use one of five editing approaches. And I’m about to walk you through each of them, how I decide which one to use, and some actual examples of what those editing approaches look like. I’m also sharing my editing best practices for any piece — no matter the approach.

## My 5 editing approaches

Here’s how I define my five main editing approaches:

*   **Overhaul**: An edit that’s almost exclusively comments to get the article directionally on track. There are usually some high-level edits in Google Docs’ Editing mode, such as rearranging the order of sections.
*   **Rework**: A 30%-50% line-by-line edit in Editing mode with overarching comments for sections that need more substantial work. Alex Lindley, our Managing Editor, is the one who initially recommended a 30% edit for pieces that need a substantial number of revisions. I’m glad he did!
*   **Deep Dive**: A line-by-line edit in Editing mode, with comments and revision requests throughout the entire article. This is easily what most content I edit falls under.
*   **Lighter Touch**: An edit where most changes are straightforward. I apply changes either directly or in Editing mode, adding comments and revision requests as needed.
*   **No Notes**: An edit where I apply all changes directly and add no commentary. These pieces are extremely rare.

I’m not normally one to coin terms — I hadn’t even thought to do so before I started writing this article. But using concrete names seems important for making sure you know what I’m talking about throughout the coming sections.

That said, you can call these editing approaches anything you want. I’m just not that precious about it.

## How I decide which editing approach to use

I choose an editing approach for an article by considering four dimensions in combination with one another:

1.   Article quality
2.   Article type
3.   Article importance
4.   Writer experience

I usually do this assessment in my head, but it translates pretty easily to a concrete framework that anyone who reviews content can use.

Here’s how it works: For the piece you’re working on, assign a score of 0 to 2 for each of the four dimensions based on the below framework. Add the scores for each column. Then add the column scores to get your total score.

0**1****2**
**Article quality**Significant issues across factual inaccuracy, tone of voice, structural coherence, clarity, search optimization, product mentions, and style guide adherence.A few issues with factual inaccuracy, tone of voice, structural coherence, clarity, search optimization, product mentions, and style guide adherence.Few if any issues with factual inaccuracy, tone of voice, structural coherence, clarity, search optimization, product mentions, and style guide adherence.
**Article type**Fully rewritten version of an existing article Refreshed version of an existing article New URL
**Article importance**Critical level Medium level Low or unsure
**Writer experience**This is a new writer. Or this writer has yet to submit a piece that’s close to expectations.The writer has a decent understanding of what their content should look like. This can come from general familiarity with the brand’s content or from feedback they’ve received.The writer has a clear understanding of how to create content that meets expectations. This can be from having substantial familiarity with the brand’s content or a longstanding relationship with the brand.
**Column scores**
**Total score**

Your total score determines which editing approach to take. That breakdown looks like this:

**Score of 0**: Overhaul

**Score of 1-2**: Rework

**Score of 3-4**: Deep Dive

**Score of 5-6**: Lighter Touch

**Scores of 7-8**: No Notes

One thing to consider is that different brands can have different definitions of what makes a high-quality article. For example, not every company is as heavily focused as Semrush on content that drives search engine and AI visibility. So, make adjustments to that row to suit your needs.

And if you just launched your website? Take out the row for article type completely to accommodate having only new URLs. Then, adjust the scale to be from 0 to 6 at your own discretion.

## The benefit of using a framework to choose an editing approach

Using a decision framework to determine an editing approach improves efficiency and reduces mental fatigue.

I can usually determine what approach I’m taking in just a few minutes, which means I automatically know what to do once I start. I don’t have to ruminate over the details of what I’ll say or adjust because that all falls into place.

And as I continue working with the same writers, their articles naturally start to have higher scores. Which means the editing goes faster. And that I don’t need to provide such extensive feedback.

For example, I usually have to explain that we use the bottom line up front (BLUF) principle — stating the main takeaway at the beginning of every section — the first time I work with a writer. But by about their third article, they know what to do based on a comment that simply says, “Let’s BLUF this paragraph.”

## What my 5 editing approaches actually look like

I frequently make copies of articles after I’ve finished reviewing them but before the writer has revised them. Most of the examples in this section come from those copies.

### Overhaul

When I’m using the Overhaul approach, I focus primarily on comments that will get the article directionally back on track.

One of the most common things I do in these sorts of articles is leave a comment over a few paragraphs or sections on how to shape the overall discussion. Like this:

![Image 1: A note by the editor on an article draft commenting on how to shape the overall discussion of the piece.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/0d/69/0d693ce2f892f86dafcad67644029d84/b1d311c8913c9dc4ffff3fe300fb90d8/image.jpeg)
If the way the sections are ordered doesn’t flow logically, I’ll either copy and paste them to the appropriate place in Editing mode or ask the writer to move the sections. It depends on how complicated the restructuring is.

### Rework

My Rework approach is how I provide enough direction and feedback for a writer to make substantial revisions without the edit taking my entire day.

One of my go-to techniques when doing a Rework is modeling what I want to see. That means I’ll heavily edit a few sections in Editing mode, explain why I made the changes I did, and then ask the writer to apply that elsewhere in the article. That’s exactly what I did here:

![Image 2: A note by the editor on an article draft explaining why certain changes were made and asking the author to apply it elsewhere in the article.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/91/13/91136115df09e98b44018599e21fe667/b59c2afb75b01e02014b5622acf6bb97/image.jpeg)
And I sometimes leave a comment at the top letting the writer know that I only edited a certain percentage of the piece. That way, they understand that I expect them to make some heavy revisions before I’m able to do more.

### Deep Dive

Most of my edits are Deep Dives. They also take the most time because I’m going through the entire piece one line at a time.

When I’m working on a Deep Dive, I move beyond addressing the most substantial issues and provide suggestions on how to strengthen arguments, better incorporate actionable workflows, and improve readability.

For example, I left this comment to explain how using a consistent sentence structure in a bulleted list improves readability:

![Image 3: A note by the editor on an article draft explaining how using a consistent sentence structure in a bulleted list improves readability.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/f3/74/f374edc7cff4a901ef98adb91aef9200/e4f6e9e96544bf46dfbc1158c913f89a/image.jpeg)
Interestingly, some of the messiest-looking Deep Dives require fewer revisions than ones that look cleaner. Why? Because there are more visible edits when I’ve used Editing mode for something I was able to phrase more succinctly compared to just a comment asking for clarity.

### Lighter Touch

Pieces where I’ve used the Lighter Touch approach can either look like I made no changes or just minimal changes — it depends on the writer and how much time I expect to have for accepting Editing mode changes later on.

In the example below, I wanted to show all changes (even minor ones) because the writer was still getting used to working with us.

![Image 4: A note by the editor on an article draft stating how a section is missing a clear BLUF statement at the start.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/79/f7/79f7031ca831d4a3820936ec77dd1b01/31a1db3c5578bffb3f2f7998d895a522/image.jpeg)
### No Notes

When I use the No Notes approach, it looks like nothing in the draft has changed after editing.

I don’t have a meaningful example of a No Notes edit to show. It would just be the Google Doc version of an article published on our blog.

But while there aren’t comments in the draft itself, I always leave comments in our project management system. Because there’s usually something the writer should be aware of, like in the example below.

![Image 5: A note by the editor on a Monday.com task giving the author general feedback along with a specific example on an article draft.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/94/e8/94e8fcf86065d7ef2626eac8fdf7a997/384417ce66282224fa93981dfeeff65d/image.jpeg)
## Best practices regardless of the editing approach

### Fact-check everything

Fact-checking is a nonnegotiable part of editing for everything that comes across my desk.

Because content I first review as an Overhaul or Rework can change substantially by the second draft, I typically only do line-by-line fact checking once I’ve received the revision.

And even if the article is great and I trust the writer, fact-checking still has to happen. It’s easy to misstate the findings from a study or say something related to SEO that’s almost true but not quite true. And those sorts of mistakes can break trust and hurt our reputation.

Common fact-checking tasks include:

*   Verifying the spellings of individuals’ and companies’ names
*   Ensuring specific numbers are supported and linking to the appropriate primary sources
*   Cross-referencing findings covered in one or our written studies with the raw data
*   Validating workflows and statements about tool features
*   Finding support for assertions about SEO and AI visibility that I’m not certain about

### Leave more feedback than you think you should

Leaving a substantial amount of feedback clarifies your expectations and helps writers understand why you’re making changes.

I’ll admit that I’ve felt uncomfortable at the number and length of comments I’ve left before. But those details make a huge difference in the quality of a writer’s future articles. Writers also appreciate feedback more than you might expect. Case in point:

![Image 6: A response by an author thanking the editor for their comments, suggestions, and edits on a Monday.com task.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/6b/67/6b67468ddf7228d365a8ebe927f17bc3/b865228435ab799e99ab16d3fe8bfe1a/image.jpeg)
Lastly, writers are able to respond when you actually provide your rationale. And they sometimes raise valid points that make you change your mind. That happens to me all the time.

### Point out what the author did well

Providing words of encouragement is great for morale and ensuring that writers know what they should keep doing.

For the article I was editing in the image below, I wanted to make sure the writer knew I liked the approach to going over the benefits of doing a Google Ads analysis:

![Image 7: A note by the editor on an article draft appreciating the author's approach of highlighting multiple benefits.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/37/89/378959c47770aba5e2ac0d97d9fe28d0/255c6d32bca899276b41903645f6460d/image.jpeg)
What about for “No notes” articles? Instead of cluttering the draft with comments, I either send a direct message to the writer or leave a comment in our project management system giving praise where it’s due.

### Ask questions

Any time you encounter a section that isn’t clear, contains unsubstantiated claims, or seems out of place, ask the writer about it.

If you come from a background in editorial like I do, it’s easy to feel like you need to fix things yourself ASAP. But it’s not a good use of your time to spend 30 minutes tracking down the source for a stat. And assuming you know what a writer is trying to convey can lead to sending the wrong message.

Asking for clarity can be as simple as this:

![Image 8: A note by the editor on an article draft asking for clarification from the author.](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/11/77/1177df98908de673441b463f5afd6a78/c1af7f07431aa840364d7f565e7f62b5/image.jpeg)
## Refine your own editing approaches

My editing approaches can benefit any content team.

That said, take what you need and leave what you don’t. Maybe you don’t publish a huge amount of content, so three editing approaches is enough.

Ultimately, I hope you walk away from this article with a clearer understanding of how to maintain a thorough review process that doesn’t become a drain on your resources and energy.

Create top-performing content

with the Semrush Content Toolkit

kept.heading: YOUNG ENTREPRENEURS ARE DELAYING DOMAIN ADOPTION, NOT ABANDONING IT (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Young entrepreneurs are starting businesses on social platforms before investing in websites and domains once they gain traction. Among 18- to 29-year-olds, domain registration interest fell from 55% in spring 2023 to 17% in spring 2026. Websites remain valued for credibility and permanence, while search visibility is a major purchase driver. More than half say AI-assisted website builders would make adoption more appealing by reducing the cost and complexity of building a web presence.
kept.article_text:
Title: Young Entrepreneurs Are Delaying Domain Adoption, Not Abandoning It

URL Source: https://circleid.com/posts/young-entrepreneurs-are-delaying-domain-adoption-not-abandoning-it

Published Time: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 23:48:23 GMT

Markdown Content:
**_Young entrepreneurs have not abandoned domain names. They are starting on social platforms first, then turning to websites as their businesses gain traction._**

A sharp decline in domain registration intent among individuals aged 18 to 29 over the past several years prompted SIDN, the registry operator of .nl and co-developer of the Hello Registry platform, to ask an important question: does this trend indicate a structural challenge for the domain name industry, or are young entrepreneurs simply following a different path towards establishing an online presence?

To find out, SIDN commissioned NielsenIQ to examine how commercially active young adults and aspiring entrepreneurs perceive websites and domain names. Surveying more than 500 respondents—half aged 18 to 29—the study provided valuable insights into how the next generation of entrepreneurs is approaching its online presence.

What emerged was not a decline in appreciation for domain names and websites, but a shift in when and how they become relevant.

Percentage by Period| Period | Total Interested in Registering | Age 18-29 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spring 2023 | 33.6% | 55.1% |
| Autumn 2023 | 29.5% | 43.8% |
| Spring 2024 | 20.7% | 41.5% |
| Autumn 2024 | 23.5% | 35.8% |
| Spring 2025 | 20.5% | 32.9% |
| Autumn 2025 | 18.8% | 19.6% |
| Spring 2026 | 16.5% | 17.4% |

#### The rise of the social-first entrepreneur

One of the clearest findings is that younger entrepreneurs no longer follow the traditional path of launching a business. A decade ago, starting a business often involved registering with the chamber of commerce, securing a domain name, creating a website and then attracting customers. Today, many young entrepreneurs begin by building an audience on social platforms. They sell products through social commerce tools, offer services via social media profiles or monetize content through creator platforms. What starts as a hobby, side project, or experiment can gradually evolve into a serious business.

Only when these activities begin to generate meaningful traction do many entrepreneurs invest in their own domain name and website. In other words, websites and domain names are no longer always the starting point of the entrepreneurial journey.

#### Domain names still matter

Perhaps the most encouraging finding for the industry is that younger adults continue to recognize the value of websites and domain names. Respondents described websites as reliable, professional and permanent digital destinations. They also value having a presence that is not dependent on algorithms, platform policies or the changing popularity of social networks.

However, independence alone is rarely enough to motivate action. The decision to register a domain name is increasingly driven by tangible business outcomes. Improved search engine discoverability was identified as one of the most important reasons to invest in a website and domain name.

The implication is clear: while younger entrepreneurs recognize the value of domain names, they expect a clear return on investment before taking the next step.

[![Image 1](https://circleid.com/images/uploads/15492_01.webp)](https://circleid.com/images/uploads/15492_01.webp)
#### Reducing friction is critical

The research also highlights another challenge familiar to many registrars and registries. For many young entrepreneurs, websites, domain names and email solutions are still perceived as relatively complex, time-consuming and expensive to implement. This perception can delay adoption, especially during the early stages of an entrepreneurial journey when simplicity and speed are paramount.

Fortunately, technology is helping to lower these barriers. More than half of respondents indicated that AI-assisted website creation tools would make the process significantly more attractive. For the domain name industry, this presents an opportunity. As AI continues to simplify website creation, some of the hurdles associated with domain adoption could disappear.

[![Image 2](https://circleid.com/images/uploads/15492_02.webp)](https://circleid.com/images/uploads/15492_02.webp)
#### What does this mean for registrars and registries?

The findings reinforce something Hello Registry and its partners are seeing more broadly across the domain name ecosystem: a substantial part of the future customer base is already commercially active, but not yet ready to invest in a traditional web presence. Rather than targeting only newly incorporated businesses, registrars may benefit from engaging individuals much earlier in their entrepreneurial journey, while they are building audiences, selling products or experimenting with online business models on social platforms.

This evolution requires a different approach. For early-stage entrepreneurs, simplicity, ease of use, integrated services and rapid deployment matter most. For growing businesses, the focus shifts toward discoverability, professionalism, conversion and long-term brand ownership. The challenge for the industry is therefore not to convince young entrepreneurs that websites matter, but to make the transition from social-first to domain-enabled entrepreneurship as seamless as possible.

#### Looking ahead

For registries, registrars and digital identity providers, the study offers an encouraging message. The next generation has not abandoned websites and domain names. On the contrary, they continue to associate them with trust, credibility, ownership and professional growth.

What has changed is the timing. Young entrepreneurs increasingly start on social platforms and migrate to domains and websites when their ambitions, audiences and businesses mature. Those organizations that understand and support this evolving customer journey will be best positioned to attract the next generation of domain name users.

kept.heading: THE NEXT HURDLE FOR AI AGENTS: GETTING WEBSITES TO LET THEM IN (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI agents like Muse and ChatGPT are able to complete tasks such as shopping and booking for users but are often blocked by websites' anti-bot systems. Some blocks are intentional while others mistakenly flag agents as malicious bots. Meta, Walmart, Stripe, and others are developing an open standard to distinguish authorized AI agents from bad bots and give businesses more control over agent access.
kept.article_text:
Title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/06/the-next-hurdle-for-ai-agents-getting-websites-to-let-them-in/

Published Time: 2026-10-06T19:56:50+00:00

Markdown Content:
Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer.

But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job.

Most recently, [Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/amazon-blocks-meta-s-muse-ai-agent-from-its-retail-site) from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog.

However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.

What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.

For instance, TechCrunch has seen a [han](https://x.com/BohuangMars/status/2107188842969362649)[d](https://x.com/BohuangMars/status/2107188842969362649)[ful](https://x.com/BohuangMars/status/2107188842969362649) of [complaints](https://x.com/buzaza/status/2107143801504731436) on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ([NBC also reported](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/ai-agent-muse-shop-e-commerce-amazon-wal-mart-wayfair-buy-rcna599069) that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)

But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was [announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/23/everything-new-coming-to-metas-ai-agent-muse/) in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.

The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.

It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.

To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun [working on an open standard](https://www.facebook.com/business/news/a-new-way-for-businesses-and-personal-agents-to-work-together) that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a [blog post.](https://www.facebook.com/business/news/a-new-way-for-businesses-and-personal-agents-to-work-together)

In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.

Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.

For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.

Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”

“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.

United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)

Early adopters’ [complaints](https://x.com/rjchint/status/2104405141130789271)[across](https://x.com/timothyfcook/status/2107174688459784435)[social](https://x.com/maulik_sh/status/2107156908356329501)[media](https://x.com/jbillow/status/2104244311256887697) have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly [blocking](https://x.com/ryanfoxeth/status/2102023108974506154) AI agents, [including](https://x.com/NanjuanS/status/2104323028058513756)[Yelp](https://x.com/RameshUtta83629/status/2105820595963531657), [eBay](https://x.com/kallasmaa/status/2107071034486849541), [Zillow](https://x.com/Aerocles/status/2106904960768291204), [Pizza Hut](https://x.com/JoshExile82/status/2106949262252941461), [Adidas](https://x.com/kesslerIO/status/2104397316673462339), [and](https://x.com/michelleoconnor/status/2107446501605838977)[various](https://x.com/akash_bhatia/status/2106527240737480719)[airlines](https://x.com/DVallota/status/2107487367984758846). Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently [increased](https://x.com/Jessicalessin/status/2106844211773595663).

A couple of people even said eBay [suspended](https://x.com/kallasmaa/status/2107071034486849541) their [accounts](https://x.com/kallasmaa/status/2107071034486849541) because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that [Google kicked out Instinct](https://x.com/jyothiwrites/status/2107493883584421973) while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.

Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its [data licensing program](https://business.yelp.com/data/). That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.

eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.

Adidas and Pizza Hut didn’t respond by the time of publication. After publication, Zillow emailed to say it allows AI agents acting on behalf of consumers, but occasionally its anti-bot measures to guard against scraping could block certain agents.

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some [suspect](https://www.threads.com/@karelbaloun/post/DdjwBeeGvR4)[that](https://x.com/TheJordude/status/2106417869764354260) Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is [attributed](https://blog.cloudflare.com/accountable-mixed-use-ai-crawlers/) to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, [Cloudflare Radar](https://radar.cloudflare.com/). The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it [now runs a marketplace](https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/01/cloudflare-launches-a-marketplace-that-lets-websites-charge-ai-bots-for-scraping/) where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing [a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/07/cloudflare-launches-kitesurf-a-browser-built-for-ai-agents/)

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s [newly announced partners](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/23/everything-new-coming-to-metas-ai-agent-muse/) haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid [expansion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/03/meta-muse-shopping-ai-agent.html), which now includes [partnered tools for small businesses](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-small-business/), a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

_Updated after publication with Zillow’s comment._
